Revue Française De Psychanalyse. XLI, 1977

Notes on the How and the Why. Jean Cournut. Pp. 481-487.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

Cournut addresses the question of discord and disagreement among analysts. He reviews the many theoretical questions about which analysts disagree and feels

160

that they sometimes get so involved in their work with the unconscious that they neglect the preconscious formations in which the Freudian system of thought is inscribed. For Cournut there were two types of questions which Freud considered. Questions concerning origins ("why" questions) led to the theory of infantile sexuality, to the search for origins in the prehistory of the infant and eventually in the prehistory of humanity. Freud's attempts to answer questions about how the psychic apparatus functioned were seen first in the Project and the early work on dream and symptom formation. These questions remained in abeyance for many years until the metapsychological papers in 1915 brought questions about how the psychic apparatus worked into prominence again. "How" questions relied on thermodynamics and neurophysiology, while the "why" questions were answered with support from anthropology and biology. Fifty years later the post-Freudians argue about the same problems. The author divides psychoanalytic writing into two classes. One group consists of clinical and auto-analytic studies which attempt to verify and refine the theory of functioning of the mental apparatus. The other group is a continuation of the search for origins and answers to "why" questions. How, then, does one choose among the various theories? The author suggests that, in a sense, such questions are concerned with an area which is "beyond psychoanalysis" and involve psychoanalysis in the larger tradition of Western humanism.

161

Psychoanalytic Essay on Orgastic Activity. Jean bergeret. Pp. 587-609.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

Bergeret is critical of studies which are too physiological to indicate much about the affective content of orgasm. Orgasm as a subject for psychoanalysis is different from the coital activity studied by physiologists. He concludes that common to both frigidity and impotence are conflicts in the fantasy experience involved at many complex levels of psychic functioning. Most studies deal with the affective experience around object relations, leading to a too exclusive consideration of the object; other studies tend to be more specifically limited to dynamic factors of instinctual origin without giving enough attention to the topographical and economic aspects of object relations. One may better evaluate orgasm by attending to the fantasies involved, for these fantasies are elaborated from very diverse instinctual and object-relational levels.

161

The title comes from Clancier's associations to the somnambulistic aspect of certain characters in the novels of Marguerite Duras. She examines the relationship

162

between orgasm and the sublimation involved in creative activity. She suggests that these creative activities are experiences at an unconscious fantasy level of identification with the creative powers of the parents. It is important that the fantasies of participation in the primal scene not be experienced as destructive, for then there may be severe inhibition in creative ability. If the individual is able to introject good parental imagoes, to know nondestructive love, he or she may be able to use these fantasies creatively.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

In contrast to the report by Chasseguet-Smirgel, Girard chooses to emphasize lacunae in Reich's theory which seem contemporary and helpful in developing a metapsychological approach to orgasm. To review Reich's work is to follow the development of a resistance to psychoanalysis, and hence his work may be helpful in showing us how to integrate orgasm into psychological theory. Reich's work was contemporary with Ferenczi's Thalassa, Rank's The Trauma of Birth, and Freud's Inhibitions, Symptoms and Anxiety and shared the vast, visionary constructions of these works. Girard reviews in detail the Reichian theory and its divergences from Freud.

The Unconscious Fantasy as Theory Agent in Psychoanalytic Treatment. Lloyd H. Silverman. Pp. 189-218.

Roderick Gilkey

Roderick Gilkey

Roderick Gilkey  

The activation of unconscious fantasies involving the gratification of symbiotic or oedipal wishes can create a positive psychotherapeutic effect. This assertion is illustrated with reference to an extended experimental research program. While insight remains the primary agent of change in psychoanalytic treatment, the activation and use of symbiotic and oedipal fantasies can also serve as important therapeutic elements. The use of such fantasy material can facilitate the process of gaining insight if such living out of the transference is occasional rather than frequent and if these experiences are ultimately interpreted at some point. This use of fantasy has been referred to in the psychoanalytic literature as transference gratifications, corrective emotional experiences, establishing a holding environment, identification with the analyst, and using the analyst as an auxiliary superego.

The Psychohistory Review. VIII, 1979

Henry James's Dream of the Louvre, "The Jolly Corner" and Psychological Interpretation. Cushing Strout. Pp. 47-52.

Peter Buckley

Peter Buckley

Peter Buckley  

Strout examines a dream of Henry James's which James described in his autobiography. The nightmare replayed a childhood visit to the Louvre. A parallel exists between this dream and his fiction, in particular his short story, "The Jolly Corner." Strout postulates that the dream is linked to James's catastrophic failures in the commercial theatre. In the dream, James turns the tables on those who rejected him in his theatrical ambitions; the person who had been made to feel like a frightened little boy when he was savagely booed on the stage became triumphant in the dream of being in the Louvre where art reverberates with the glory of Napoleonic conquest. Parallel themes are seen in "The Jolly Corner" and in James's essay, "The American Scene." The author suggests that the dream reflects a Napoleonic conquest through popular success on the stage. It is significant that at the end of his life James suffered from the delusion (due to an organic mental syndrome) that he was indeed Napoleon.

169

The Psychohistory Review. VIII, 1979

A Note on the Adaptation of the Psychoanalytic Method to the Study of Historical Personalities: Psychoanalysts on Schreber. Carl Pletsch. Pp. 46-50.

Peter Buckley

Peter Buckley

Peter Buckley  

The author suggests that in the psychological study of historical personalities, what historians most want from psychoanalysis is its method rather than its theory. He examines two recent books on Schreber (William G. Niederland's The

169

Schreber Case: Psychoanalytic Profile of a Paranoid Personality and M. Schatzman's Soul Murder: Persecution in the Family), in order to investigate how psychoanalysis has been adapted to the study of this historical person. He notes that the principal focus of Niederland's book was the relationship between the mental illness of Schreber and the child-rearing theories of his father. Niederland drew the theoretical conclusion that Freud was right both in his diagnosis of Schreber and in his theory of paranoia. From the same information, Schatzman concluded that Freud was wrong and that Schreber's fear that his soul was being murdered by a god who used him as a passive female sex object was not so much the consequence of repressed homosexual love for his father as of the repressed fears of his father's very real persecution of him as a child. The author of this paper believes that this conclusion is a consequence of Schatzman's identification with Schreber and that the historian who sets out to explore the psychoanalytic aspects of any historical problem must be aware that there is almost certainly an unconscious dimension to his choice. Niederland's book illustrates how an analyst may continue to derive new insight from a finite quantity of written sources. Schreber's memoirs serve the function of providing primary "clinical" evidence, while his father's writings enable an objective reconstruction of Schreber's childhood experiences to be made which can then be correlated with Schreber's fantasies. The author concludes that when a significant amount of fantasy material is available, along with the possibility of acquiring information about the parents and intimate associates of the historical figure in question, the principal difficulties involved in the analysis of historical personalities can be resolved. The historian-analyst has to substitute the historical analysand's transference-like relationships to his contemporaries for the unattainable transference relationship with the analyst.

170

H. Blank  

A frequent pattern of associations in the analyses of narcissistic patients seems to be the counterpart of the child's use of denial in fantasy to ward off feelings of weakness and insecurity. These patients have failed to master the latency task of developing tolerance for tension, frustration, and uncertainty. This tends to produce impasses in their treatment. An approach to this problem is outlined: it begins with focus on present-day problems of impulse control and failures of frustration tolerance. The aim is to awaken hope for the development of genuine self-control that had been abandoned in the postoedipal period.

Reflections on the Psychoanalytic Process and Its Therapeutic Potential. Hans W. Loewald. Pp. 155-167.

H. Blank

H. Blank

H. Blank  

The insufficiently recognized factors that determine therapeutic potential are first examined pragmatically. Among these are the analyst's breadth of life experience and imagination, the manner in which intercurrent events in the patient's life are handled, and the use of educational measures, encouragement, and reassurance. The psychoanalytic process is then examined from a strictly psychoanalytic viewpoint. Of crucial importance is the patient-analyst relationship and the nature of the analyst's empathic objectivity. In treating the transference neuroses, unless the analyst's own oedipal conflicts are being repeatedly mastered, true empathy with patients' unresolved conflicts cannot take place, and the analyst's interpretations, however correct as to abstract content, are not likely to reach the patients so that they can make them their own. This paradigm holds true also for the more serious narcissistic disorders and borderline states. The analyst's ability to recognize and work with disturbances originating in the preoedipal years depends on his/her awareness and mastery of his/her own problems in these depths.

330

Magna Est Vis Veritatis Tuae et Praevalebit. John E. Gedo. Pp. 53-82.

Melvin Stanger

Melvin Stanger

Melvin Stanger  

This is an attempt by the author to better understand the break between Sigmund Freud and Carl Jung through a study of the recently published correspondence between them. The title of Gedo's paper is, in fact, a quotation from a letter of Jung to Freud dated November 11, 1908: "Great is the power of thy truth and it will prevail." Using the Freud-Jung correspondence, Gedo illustrates, quite correctly I feel, that Jung needed Freud as an idealized and

474

God-like object. This was incompatible with Freud's requirements of Jung, since Freud wished Jung to be his successor/son. Jung felt that this was too much for him and that it was incompatible with his real interests. Freud's rejection of the role wished on him by Jung and his disavowal of Jung's aims ("You mustn't regard me as the founder of a religion") led to feelings of disillusionment, devaluation, and narcissistic rage on Jung's part. Gedo's explication seems reasonable, but appears to be incomplete, since it is based essentially on psychodynamics involving only the narcissistic conflicts that were present. No attempt is made to integrate narcissistic vicissitudes with drives. For example, I would strongly argue that Jung's need for a God-like father was a defensive retreat from the anxiety associated with his unacceptable wishes toward a real-life father and that he was threatened in his relationship with Freud precisely because of the increasing strength of his displaced parricidal and homosexual wishes.

475

In a brief beginning section, the authors review their work toward the elimination of metapsychology and its replacement by a "psychoanalytic phenomenology." Various aspects of the representational world comprise the necessary elements of this psychology, including specific configurations of self and object, developmental tasks, and conscious and unconscious motivations. The authors further assert that the "need to maintain the organization of experience is a central motivational principle in the patterning of human conduct." This fundamental relationship between experience and conduct is the stated focus for the clinical material presented later in the paper. The disappearance of the self-destructive symptoms this patient presented is conceptualized as the effect of the patient's reliance on the therapist as a "self-object," which resulted in the maintenance of her psychological organization as a stable, cohesive, and embodied self.

Losserand reviews Freud's concept of epilepsy as elaborated in his Dostoevsky article. He sees the origin of the Freudian concept in Charcot's ideas on hysteria major. Charcot felt that hysteria and epilepsy were coeval, developing

669

at the same time. Losserand reviews the historical development of neurological and psychological conceptualizations of hysteria, epilepsy, and hystero-epilepsy. These scientific concepts of epilepsy are traced through Charcot's work, the early papers of Freud on the etiology of hysteria, and the work of French medical writers such as Trousseau and Babinski. Losserand attempts to delineate the complex relationship between hysterical attack, epileptic seizure, and coitus, as suggested in Freud's article on Dostoevsky. In the final section the author discusses The Brothers Karamazov, speculating on the psychological significance of various personages in the novel. He is especially concerned with the relationship of Smerdiakov and Alyosha.

December 9, 1980. ANNA FREUD ON VIDEOTAPE: CHILD ANALYSIS AS THE STUDY OF MENTAL GROWTH (NORMAL AND ABNORMAL).

In a videotaped lecture, Anna Freud presented an unpublished paper which, she said, was of necessity very condensed and without clinical examples. The paper was divided into three sections. The first comprised an international survey of child analytic work, subdivided as follows:

1. The starting point of child analysis was the Little Hans case history, which gave rise to various attempts at treatment and prevention. Miss Freud noted that some innovative and interesting experiments have been lost, along with their innovators.

2. There have been numerous efforts to develop techniques suitable for child analysis. Children, because of id pressures, lack of ego development, poorly developed working alliances, and unusual transferences, are not usually suited for classical free association.

3. There has been a tendency to follow the mainstream of adult psychoanalysis, as in the "widening scope," with application to conditions such as borderline, autism, and infantile psychosis.

4. Another tendency has involved considering whether child analysis and direct observation of children by child analysts could confirm, refute, or amend the findings of adult analysis.

5. There has been the hope, about which Miss Freud has not been optimistic, that child analysis would break new ground in adult analysis.

6. There has been a trend to study earlier and earlier life stages to find the chronological and developmental period most important for the origin of pathology. This is a tendency which Miss Freud feels has led to unfortunate specialization of interest and divergencies of theory.

The author's threefold purpose in this detailed investigation is (1) to amplify a basic element in the methodology of psychoanalytic iconography that was applied in his earlier Michelangelo study; (2) to illuminate the representation of certain unresolved conflicts which were fundamental determinants of both the

form and content of images that Michelangelo created in a single decade of his work; and (3) to speculate on the developmental process of the "splitting" of the maternal object representation into the idealized Madonna figure and the abandoning, murderous Medea figure. This interesting paper, enriched with several clinical examples, dovetails nicely with the earlier paper by Peter Blos. The author examines the resurgence of preoedipal ties to the mother in girls whose mothers were unable to meet their dependency needs when they were infants. It is suggested that "a girl in early adolescence feels empty and depressed if her preoedipal love object was ambivalent about her and if her dependency needs were unmet." Case histories are presented of a few girls who dealt with conflicts of this type through delinquent actions. Some suggestions are made about the therapeutic approaches to various types of delinquent girls and their mothers.

Preschool Children's Conception of Ghosts. Theodore Shapiro; Miriam Sherman; Irving Osowsky. Pp. 41-55.

This investigation attempts to clarify three- and four-year-old children's perceptions of ghosts and their relation to the hypothesis of the "floating ghost" as an early infantile remembrance. It appears to confirm the notion that young children's representation of ghosts results from an admixture of learned conscious ideas regarding ghosts and an ill-defined part which is based upon primitive unconscious ideas about the unknown stranger and the mysterious images of earlier nightly visits from father and mother.

Journal of the American Academy of Child Psychiatry. XIX, 1980

Parental Loss Antecedent to Childhood Diabetes Mellitus. David R. Leaverton, et al. Pp. 678-689.

There is evidence that relates life stress to the onset of juvenile diabetes mellitus. Parental loss and other stresses are documented in this study of thirty-seven children with diabetes and their families. Divorce, separation, or death of the child's parents was recorded through home interviews. Children with insulindependent diabetes within one geographic area were included. Comparison with children without diabetes matches for age, sex, race, geographic area, and socioeconomic status showed that parental loss was significantly higher in the children who later developed diabetes. Children of disrupted families were recurrently hospitalized, while children of stable families were not. Results of this study have implications relative to etiology of diabetes as well as to preventive mental health measures.

DISCUSSION: Dr. Harold P. Blum discussed the current proposals for changes of technique related to controversies surrounding developmental concepts, including the relative role of deficit and conflict. He spoke about those analysts who emphasize preoedipal conflicts and those analysts who address themselves to the centrality of oedipal conflicts even in cases of severe pathology. Dr. Blum also pointed out the importance of differentiating between arrest and regression and problems encountered in attempts to analyze deficit and to promote structural development. Dr. Simon Grolnick saw development as complex, circular, actually spiral, and not linear. He addressed himself to the controversy of whether analysis provides an opportunity for new developmental change. He saw the developmental process as continuously interweaving regressive, progressive, and adaptive factors at higher and higher symbolic and internalized levels throughout life. Dr. Melvin A. Scharfman referred to development as evolving from the interaction of biological potential and the environment. Where developmental lag exists, it may be that in the course of analysis interferences with that developmental process may be removed and the child may reach a new developmental level. In that context the analyst may be used by the child as a new object at a developmental level not previously achieved, but the analyst does nothing to promote that other than maintain an analytic stance.

DISCUSSION: Dr. George H. Wiedeman addressed Dr. Eisnitz's concept of the self representation in its relationship to structural theory. He pointed out that Dr. Eisnitz described the self representation as a system within the ego, but also as an organizing influence on the function of the ego, referring to it as a "final common pathway of interaction between id, ego, and superego." This makes it seem a higher level or superordinate concept in respect to its relationship to the system ego. Dr. Wiedeman questioned whether the self representation can be seen as a part of the structural ego and pointed out that this view of it might seem inconsistent unless the ego is defined not as a part of the psychic organization, but as a term more closely akin to concepts such as "self" or to Freud's "Ich," which may refer to the total living being. Dr. Wiedeman commented upon the relationship between Dr. Eisnitz's concept of the self representation and the sociological concept of social roles. Dr. Eisnitz had described units of the basic self representation being cathected or decathected in accordance with the demands of both the intrapsychic and the external environment. Dr. Wiedeman pointed out that these units of the self representation are the intrapsychic processes or components which influence the effective or conflicted performance of social roles and thus determine overt behavior. Dr. Charles S. Tolk questioned whether the instability of the self representation as described by Dr. Eisnitz, particularly in Cases 2 and 3, should be considered the major issue involved in these patients' self-esteem problems and feelings of weakness, self-criticism, and emptiness. Could these difficulties not be viewed as pathological forms of self-esteem regulation or as the consequence of superego pathology?

The narcissistic personality, one that internalizes object relations, seems aloof from involvement with others, unless they adore him, yet needs intensely to have his grandiose self supported by their regard. This paper describes how such a person reinforces the cohesiveness of his grandiose self and what happens when he becomes a leader. The example chosen is that of Ataturk and the relationship between his personality and his need to repair the injuries suffered by his followers.

DISCUSSION: Dr. Ira Mintz presented several dramatic examples of anniversary reactions and said that patients are often unaware of the connection between the important anniversary and the onset of physical illness or the exacerbation of symptoms. The role of the unconscious meaning of events must be explored if we are to understand these phenomena in more than just a superficial way. In

490

evaluating neuroendocrine studies, we must understand that organic vulnerability may be an important factor, but it is not sufficient to explain psychosomatic phenomena. In Luparello's work, asthmatic attacks were induced and aborted with the same saline solution, first described to the patient as allergenic and then as medicated. Dr. Mintz then described three patients with severe ulcerative colitis. In their treatment, bouts of negative transference produced attacks of colitis; effective interpretations resulted in a cessation of the attacks. Stubborn episodes of severe bleeding in all three patients responded dramatically to interpretation. In these patients, when changes occurred in the transference, in the defensive systems, in object relations, in the tendency to regress, and in the capacity to tolerate frustration and emotional distress, there were also changing endocrine responses related to the cessation of symptoms. The crucial feature was the clinical responsiveness to interpretation. This responsiveness occurred regardless of the additional multidetermined genetic and physiological factors intimately associated with the disease. Dr. Howard Schwartz addressed what he called the problem of "the subtle and overt resistances to the treatment of psychosomatic patients among many analysts." He noted that the medical profession is paying increasing attention to the role of psychological factors in medical disease, even as the psychoanalytic profession seems to be losing interest in psychosomatics. While agreeing with Dr. Deutsch that there is an overly simplified and antiquated view of the principles involved in treating patients with psychosomatic illnesses, Dr. Schwartz emphasized an additional psychological factor in the apparent reluctance analysts have to treat these patients. While we have been willing to expand the scope of analysis to include borderline, narcissistic, and severe character pathology, we have been less willing to include "psychosomatically ill patients with similar, if not identical, ego weaknesses and preoedipal arrests and fixations." Such an avoidance represents a form of denial; in essence we are looking away to avoid a danger. The danger is the fantasied loss of an aspect of our professional identity. In becoming analysts we have given up, and often painfully mourned, aspects of our identities as physicians. We are afraid that the treatment of psychosomatic patients, with its use of parameters and the frequent need for shared management, would severely compromise our technique and hence our identity as analysts. We would no longer be "analysts," but instead "practitioners of psychoanalytic psychotherapy." To avoid this danger, we avoid treating these patients. Dr. Schwartz suggested that a working out of internal conflicts connected with the treatment of psychosomatic patients might allow more of us to feel comfortable treating these patients, with all the analytic skills we can bring to bear and with a comfortable recognition that shared management of such patients need not unduly compromise analytic work.

491

Sheila Gray

Sheila Gray

Sheila Gray  

The authors have reviewed selected publications and videotapes of the actual work of several psychoanalysts who are prominently identified with short-term

483

dynamic psychotherapy, and they propose an explanation for their success which would go beyond the concept of transference cure. They suggest that these treatments are as effective as psychoanalysis proper because accurate deep interpretations are, in fact, made. In short-term dynamic psychotherapy, however, the therapist utilizes some important modifications of classical psychoanalytic technique to make such interpretations acceptable to the patient. Examples of these modified techniques include the rapid juxtaposition of genetic and concurrent events with transference interpretation, active disconfirmation of the patient's transferential view of the therapist, and active expression of empathy and emotional support. The authors suggest that recent theories of memory as creative reconstruction do away with earlier concerns that such comments may prove to be inexact interpretations, and so make short-term work credible. There follows a long but incomplete bibliography on this topic.

Thrane, a philosopher by training and profession, begins with an analysis of shame, using the points of view and data supplied by psychoanalysis, anthropology, and philosophy, which helps us to understand shame in a more comprehensive way. The author then goes on to offer a theory of the function of the sense of shame, involving the relationship to a coherent and meaningful sense of self. This enables us to appreciate the function of shame as an adaptation. Thrane concludes with remarks concerning the understanding of shame in the practice of psychotherapy, particularly in its relevance to respect for the patient's individuality.

Ronald Krasner

Ronald Krasner

Ronald Krasner  

The author, considering supervision as one of the cornerstones of psychoanalytic education, attempts to shed light on the dynamics of the supervisory experience. He posits an ongoing process in the supervisor-therapist relationship similar to that in the therapist-patient relationship and identifies this as the parallel process. The experimental design employed to study this phenomenon consisted of supervision by the author of the two therapists, a man and a woman candidate, and the author's participation in a peer supervisory group in which tapes of the supervisory hours were used. From a case example given, several inferences are drawn: that this process is "probably always there"; that the controlling variable is the supervisor; that there is simultaneous transference and countertransference operative for patient, therapist, and supervisor; and that the "overlapping" of these transferences creates the parallel process. In a theoretical discussion of these observations, the author mentions the tension that exists between the "didactic" and the "emotional" process of learning. Sullivan's concept of participation-observation is discussed in its application to parallel process, and in the realm of field theory the "reciprocal process" ("the interpersonal response evoked in the recipient in the parallel process") is briefly cited.

The relation between language and internal psychic reality, with special emphasis on the linguistic productions of schizophrenics, is explored. The author reviews Paul Ricoeur's conceptions of psychoanalysis as a science and his ideas on the origin, structure, and function of psychic facts. He then compares them to Sullivan's notions of language and meaning. Both Ricoeur and Sullivan, Glass feels, consider language as constituting "critical evidence; it is the basis for data which allows the observer to encircle the self with explanation." Meaning invariably can be derived from utterance, which in turn contains significant psychic fact. Such facts, which according to Ricoeur symbolize unconscious structure, can be retrieved and identified through a "therapeutic transference." They represent internal reality and are present in the narrative of the subject's experience.

Individual and Family Therapy: Toward an Integration

By Fred M. Sander, M.D. New York/London: Aronson, 1979. 242 pp.

Judith Wallerstein

Judith Wallerstein

Judith S. Wallerstein
CORTE MADERA, CALIF.

Judith Wallerstein  

Reading this well written, lively, complexly textured book, one has the persistent sense of being in the presence of a gifted teacher who is able to weave together a wide range of psychological themes. These are drawn from clinical practice, from psychological and psychoanalytic theory, and from a long-standing familiarity with literature, especially the literature of the theater. One obtains the impression that the author was prevailed upon by admiring students to bring his lectures together into a book. The book skillfully combines an overview of individual psychology and individual psychotherapy, family systems theory and family therapy, and a wide range of timely social and professional issues, including the contemporary trend toward childlessness, communication theory in schizophrenia, and some aspects of the current interest in narcissism.

These perspectives are illustrated and enhanced by references to works of literature, drawn primarily from the theater. Sander has the engaging notion that the theatrical play represents an apt vehicle of choice for the representation of intrafamilial and interpersonal perspectives. In such literary works he sees the early surfacing of certain community concerns and professional advances. For instance, he views T. S. Eliot's The Cocktail Party as a statement of the increasing isolation and instability of the modern family, which presaged the rise of the family therapy movement.

Meetings of the New York Psychoanalytic Society

November 11, 1980. MODIFICATIONS IN THE TRADITIONAL PSYCHOANALYTIC THEORY OF FEMALE ADOLESCENT DEVELOPMENT. Peter Blos, Ph.D.

Classical psychoanalytic theory requires alignment with newer findings. Freud's original formulations were derived from the treatment of adults; new research in the field of direct child and infant observation forces us to take a fresh look at traditional theory. A major issue has been the question of whether femininity is a purely defensive structure, secondary to the vicissitudes of penis envy. Dr. Blos gave a careful restatement of Freud's formulations of the path toward femininity, in order to review critically some of the basic assumptions.

Current research indicates that gender identity occurs earlier than previously thought. Stoller's opinion is that core gender identity has its roots in the first year; much data also exists to the effect that neonates show observable sex-linked differences. In addition, it is now clear that genital awareness and excitability, as well as the child's awareness of genital difference, also occur at a much younger age than was previously thought. Penis envy is aroused defensively to ward off regression to and aggression against the early mother who is bound to frustrate and disappoint her child. The infantile experience of incompleteness, with the ensuing aggression toward the mother, are handled differently by boys and girls; the girl tends to deflect her aggression toward the acquisition of a body part, the penis, which merges symbolically with the representation of the lost breast. The girl's wish for the breast thus becomes shunted onto a masculine track in order to avoid the regressive pull to primary passivity and in order to avoid aggressively harming the mother. The masculinity complex as seen in adolescence reveals an unresolved ambivalence conflict with the preoedipal mother.

From working with adolescents, one sees that the most profound and obdurate complex resides in the boy's attachment to his father and the girl's preoedipal bond with her mother. The negative oedipus complex is enmeshed in the etiology of every adolescent emotional disturbance. The adolescent girl, however, tolerates a greater fluidity between the infantile attachments to her parents and her adult personality consolidation than does the boy. The girl's normal ambivalence toward the preoedipal mother is reactivated during adolescence. The little girl had once escaped this intense ambivalence by a flight to the father, who was not contaminated by the chaotic-archaic ambitendencies of her early relationship to her mother. In adolescence, the girl may, under the sway of the regressive pull to the early mother, again turn frantically to the other sex. Dr. Blos calls this pseudo-heterosexuality the "oedipal defense." The turn to true femininity occurs later—only after identification with mother's maternal function. This step can be interfered with by a mother's need for closeness and her inability to allow for her daughter's autonomy.

Autoerotism. Jean Gillibert. Pp. 769-949.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

This is a long dissertation on autoerotism in its relationship to libido, narcissism, and the death instinct. Gillibert attempts to develop a metapsychology of autoerotism, and, as one commentator suggests, he develops a "metalanguage" of autoerotism. The general thesis is that autoerotism is the keystone of the theory of sexuality as a specific dimension of human sexuality. For Gillibert, autoerotism demarcates the sexual impulse from the self-preservation instinct. Further, libido is opposed to the death instinct, but the death instinct and its derivatives are immanent. From this Gillibert proceeds to a focus on what he terms the "inert." One of the negative modalities of autoerotism develops following the necrophagic incorporation of the dead father. The incorporated cadaver is an example of the inert. Gillibert illustrates the theme of the inert with Don Giovanni and the statue of the Commendatore. Autoerotism as exemplified by Don Giovanni takes on an autodestructive form, that of a masochistic orgy and an autoerotic madness which overwhelms the ego. This aspect of autoerotism in which there is an unconscious fantasy of possession by the dead father is derived by Gillibert from his work with psychotics. He also discusses the autoerotic behavior of autistic children. The essay is followed by brief comments and discussions delivered by participants in the Thirty-Seventh Congress of Romance Language Psychoanalysts.

The authors review some of the legal, ethical, and technical problems in supervised psychoanalysis and psychotherapy. They conclude that while it is ethically necessary to obtain the patient's permission to consult a supervisor, the patient's knowledge that a supervisor is involved in the case may lead to an unanalyzable distortion of the therapeutic relationship. To resolve this conflict, they propose that the psychoanalyst routinely obtain written permission for future consultation at the very outset of treatment and not allude to it thereafter. This technique would, the authors believe, allow any questions the patient raises about consultation in the course of treatment to be addressed interpretatively.

Lerner reviews some early and recent definitions of the concept of penis envy. She concedes that the perception of actual anatomical differences between the sexes does play a role in little girls' psychic development, but she believes it is precipitated not so much by the experience that the male organ is superior as by a need to deal defensively with the anxieties and conflicts aroused by her own genitals. She recommends that the specific meaning of penis envy must be elucidated in each case.

Reder and Tyson consolidated the data from all studies of dropout from psychotherapy and psychoanalysis reported since 1930 and re-evaluated this material from a variety of viewpoints. They found that consistently the patient dropout rate is initially high and then falls off appreciably after a few weeks of treatment. They see this as a confirmation of the wisdom of Freud's recommendation

165

that there be an initial trial period and a re-evaluation prior to embarking on a lengthy psychoanalysis.

The author explicitly outlines the rights which he believes essential for the psychiatrist in order to assure ethical and competent professional performance: (1) the right to form an independent opinion; (2) the right to define personal and professional limitations; (3) the right to formulate a treatment plan that is expected to be effective in achieving explicit goals; (4) the right to define the characteristics of the clinical setting that will best serve the purpose of goal achievement; (5) the right to consult with colleagues; (6) the right to maintain undisclosed the observations, thoughts, formulations, and predictions about the patient; and (7) the right to terminate responsibility for the treatment and care of a patient with reasonable notification and assistance in finding other professional services. Collins points out that these rights are not opposed to those of the patient or of society in general, but, rather, enhance them and facilitate the patient's gaining access to appropriate care and treatment.

The author suggests that while borderline and narcissistic patients may exhibit different psychopathology and life-adjustments, they seem to have similar disorders of affects and moods. He identifies several such disturbances: (1) a sense of inappropriateness, a contradiction between what is reported and what is experienced; (2) a sense of injustice, prevalent among narcissistic patients, or of alienation, prevalent among borderline patients; (3) a pervasive sense of boredom characterized by perceptual ambiguity and a sense of being locked into an eternal, meaningless present; (4) overt anger; (5) depersonalization; (6) a sense of emptiness, which the author traces to the fragmentation and dispersal of affects which these patients experience. Hartocollis recommends that disturbances of affect, viewed in a developmental hierarchy, may be used as clues to diagnosis, and as the basis for prescribing medication. They can also form the focus of interpretations in the context of an established psychotherapeutic relationship.

William James's Eyes: The Thought Behind the Man. H. M. Greenspan. Pp. 26-46.

Peter Buckley

Peter Buckley

Peter Buckley  

This paper views William James's work as an active and intentional confrontation with life-historical experience. The metaphor of vision is seen to figure centrally in James's psychological and philosophical writings. The author connects the visual metaphors in his work with the eye troubles that he suffered from during the period 1865 to 1885. He notes that health and the ability "to see" were virtually synonymous in James's writing on psychopathology and that his scholarly work focused on extending "the field of vision." "Visions of horror" were also a central element of his transient emotional crisis which was very similar in nature to his father's breakdown twenty-five years earlier. Significantly, his eye problems abated following his editing and arranging the publication of his father's literary remains. The author concludes that the issue of seeing was the constitutive passion of James's life just as it formed the constitutive imagery of his thought.

The Sins of the Parents: The Borderline Adolescent and Primal Confusion. Peter L. Giovacchini. Pp. 213-233.

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman  

Giovacchini redefines his particular use of the term, borderline, as different from the broader definitions of Masterson and Kernberg. The patients he calls borderline suffer from "a pervasive sense of inadequacy and helplessness" that results from primitive developmental fixations "involving symbiotic and even presymbiotic stages." The author describes the behavior in therapy of a mother and her grown children (all borderline as he defines it), suggesting that this behavior indicates the very early level of ego deficit in these people. He observes that the mother's striking inability to recognize her own bodily clues and those of her children deprived the children (as she herself was probably deprived in her own infancy) of the ability to learn the most basic recognition and control of their own drives. In order to have any chance to alter this painful, difficult situation, the therapist must avoid countertransference reactions which repeat the early jarring environment, but must create a "holding environment" which will, it is to be hoped, give the patient a second chance at development.

Childhood and Adolescent Development of Ten Female Prostitutes. Katherine MacVicar and Marcia Dillon. Pp. 145-159.

The study of ten adolescent and young adult female prostitutes revealed that three of them had schizophrenic psychoses, while the remainder had borderline character structures. The psychotic adolescents participated in prostitution in an attempt to preserve some vestige of object relationships. The borderline adolescents, all of whom had chaotic family histories, had severe splits in the world of self and object, with the result that all-good and all-bad images were kept apart. The all-good image was that of the pimp, while the all-bad image was that of the customer. Other aspects of prostitution such as the high incidence of suicide attempts, homosexuality, and the use of money are also discussed.

Successful Psychotherapy of Severe Emotional Disturbance in a Young Retarded Boy. Donald S. Gair; Charles Hersch; Shirley Wiesenfeld. Pp. 257-269.

The development of a boy who at age six was diagnosed as having "an emotional form of retardation" and "psychosis" is reported and followed to adulthood. Initially untestable for IQ, he ultimately tested stably low in the mildly retarded range. At referral he showed severe deficiencies in ego development. He improved following several years of psychotherapy and concurrent casework with the parents. At age twenty-seven he was still mildly retarded, but self-supporting and free of significant personality disabilities. This presentation both exemplifies the usefulness of psychotherapy and family casework in the treatment of a retarded child, and strongly supports the growing reinvestment in mental retardation by psychiatry and child psychiatry.

DISCUSSION: Dr. Aaron H. Esman agreed with Dr. Pine's main thesis. However, he disputed Dr. Pine's tendency to give the "phase" concept an objective reality it does not have. Development is a continuous, seamless flux. The segments into which the observer partitions it refer to his purposes and so are, of necessity, arbitrary. "Phases" are merely the constructs of the observer. But in this context, Dr. Pine's stress on "moments" is important. It allows for a heuristic designation of a coherent pattern of responses, behavior, fantasies, and interactions, without the assumption that it embraces the totality of the child's psychophysiological repertoire. Dr. Esman agreed that the ideas "normal symbiosis" and "undifferentiated phase" should be retained, recognizing these terms as relative designations of complex psychobiological states. Infants have perceptual and discriminatory capacities far beyond what we used to think. But an infant's ability at any given moment to use these capacities is a function of his "state.

Change in Psychoanalytic Treatment. Judd Marmor. Pp. 345-357.

Roderick Gilkey

Roderick Gilkey

Roderick Gilkey  

Marmor explores the nature of change in psychoanalytic treatment. Traditionally, the increase in cognitive awareness (insight) and the release of repressed affect (abreaction) have been viewed as the primary factors associated with change. Freud, however, made it clear that these factors were in themselves insufficient agents of change; increasingly, he came to emphasize the importance of the working through of resistances. The length of time required for a successful analysis is not, in Marmor's view, due to the duration of the uncovering process. Rather it is due to the amount of time required for the patient to generalize insights gained in the transference encounter and to apply them to life situations. This involves the interpretation and ultimate working through of "perceptual distortions and defensive rationalizations under an umbrella of benign and consistent emotional support.

Feinstein notes the ubiquitous presence of emotional illness in the James family and examines the secondary gain that was obtained from it. He observes that in addition to serving as an unconscious justification for the pleasure of travel and leisure, invalidism could also convey ambivalent feelings that were proscribed by the social ideal of the Victorian family. The paper examines the expression of such invalidism among the various members of the James family and suggests that it was a compromise between the attainment of forbidden goals and unconscious punishment for that attainment.

The Psychohistory Review. VIII, 1979

Revision of a Chapter in the Life of Henry James. Leon Edel. Pp. 23-25.

Peter Buckley

Peter Buckley

Peter Buckley  

This revision of the beginning of a chapter in Edel's life of Henry James deals with the psychological impact of William James's marriage upon his younger brother. Edel quotes Henry as congratulating William in the following fashion: "I have just heard from Mother that you have decided to be married on the 10th ult. and as I was divorced from you by an untimely fate on this occasion, let me at least repair the injury by giving you, in the most earnest words that my clumsy pen can shape, a tender bridal benediction." Edel suggests that the deeper feelings implicit in the word "divorce" were written into Henry's novel, Confidence, which deals with a friendship between two young men. James casts his brother in the character of Gordon Wright, a young scientist who wishes to marry a woman named Angela. Wright asks his aesthetic and analytical friend to give his opinion of Angela and is told that she is not his sort. Wright takes his advice seriously and marries on the rebound a flighty unsuitable woman. Edel points out that in this fantasy, Henry James not only appoints himself advisor to his brother on his marriage, but has him make a marriage from which Henry must rescue him. Finally, the Henry James figure falls in love with Angela.

In this article Emma Goldman's political career is viewed as an expression of her family conflicts. Wexler concludes that Goldman's adoption of anarchist beliefs was a means of separating herself from her parents and expressing hostility toward all of their expectations while simultaneously identifying with her father's curse that she was a disgrace to the family and a loose woman. Her adoption of anarchism was her means of attacking the world of her parents and at the same time attacking those institutions, such as the state and religion, which she believed had exploited them. It also allowed her in a creative way to transform her latent feelings of guilt toward the dead brother of her childhood into a fantasy of rescuing him while also becoming a martyr like him.

Meetings of the New York Psychoanalytic Society

March 11, 1980. THE PSYCHOANALYTIC THEORY OF THE DRIVES. Charles Brenner, M.D.

Dr. Brenner emphasized the fundamental importance of the role of the drives in psychoanalytic theory and the fact that the nature of the concept of the drives has often been misunderstood. He quoted Freud as saying, "The theory of the [instinctual drives] is so to say our mythology. Instincts are mythical entities, magnificent in their indefiniteness. In our work we cannot for a moment disregard them, yet we are never sure that we are seeing them clearly." The speaker subsequently proposed a substantial revision of Freud's theory of the nature and source of the drives, hoping to offer a more definite and less mythical view of some aspects of drive theory.

Dr. Brenner pointed out that Freud thought of the mind as an apparatus that deals with stimuli. The stimuli that activate the mental apparatus are of two sorts, sensory stimuli from the environment and bodily stimuli of a special kind. These latter Freud called drives for the reason that they impel or drive the mental apparatus to activity in accordance with the pleasure principle. It was Freud's conviction that the sources of the drives were somatic and not psychic. This idea of the drive as a frontier phenomenon, as something somatopsychic whose source is somatic and whose effect is psychic, is one which Freud maintaied throughout the course of the development of his drive theory. Freud described somatic origins for both libido and aggression. The erogenous zones are the source of the libido. As for aggression, the source, according to Freud, is a biological death drive common to all living matter. Dr. Brenner stated that Freud did not want to rely on psychoanalytic data for the part of his libido theory that has to do with its somatic source or origin. He believed that reliable data could come only from other sources, such as observation of sexual behavior, a better knowledge of the nature and function of sexual hormones, comparative physiological and anatomical studies, and the like. The connections between libido as a driving force in mental life and those parts of the body Freud designated as erogenous zones are indisputable. Dr. Brenner pointed out, however, that there is as yet no reliable evidence of endocrine or other changes in the genital apparatus itself to support Freud's theory that the phallic-genital zone is a source of libido as a driving force in psychic life. There is no doubt that the stimulation of any of the important zones can increase the urgency of libidinal wishes, but to recognize this is quite different from asserting that these zones are the source of libido as a constant driving force in mental life.

DISCUSSION: Dr. Benjamin B. Rubinstein felt that Dr. Brenner had failed to note that Freud had asked himself how we can explain the impelling character of drives, perhaps the most fundamental question of any drive theory. Freud's answer in regard to the libidinal drives was based on two principal notions: 1) the constancy principle, the postulate that the central nervous system, including the mental apparatus, has a built-in tendency to maintain its excitation at as low a level as possible, which ideally is the zero level; and 2) the hypothesis that the level of excitation in the mental apparatus is continually raised by somatic stimulation arising in the erogenous zones. Through the clash of these opposing forces the system somehow develops the means to drain off the excitation and to inhibit at their source the production of the somatic stimuli that cause it. Dr. Rubinstein pointed out that Dr. Brenner had chosen to ignore what most likely was Freud's major reason for advancing his theory: to explain the impelling character of the drives. Instead, Dr. Brenner focused on one element of the construction, namely the hypothesis of the somatic stimulation. Dr. Rubinstein agreed with Dr. Brenner that this hypothesis has turned out to be mistaken, but neither psychoanalytic nor behavioral data can explain the impelling character of the drives. The most such data can show is that the phenomena that constitute these data appear as if a factor has acquired its impelling character.

September 16, 1980. THE "UNOBJECTIONABLE" COMPONENT OF THE TRANSFERENCE. Martin H. Stein, M.D.

The so-called "unobjectionable" component of the transference, which allows the patient to cooperate in the analytic process, has been described as the "working alliance" (Greenson) and the "therapeutic alliance" (Zetzel). Dr. Stein acknowledged that such concepts have entered common parlance, but he raised questions about their usefulness. He illustrated his doubts with a clinical description of a group of patients. These are patients who take to analysis easily and are typically neurotic, young, and intelligent. Their transference is predominantly positive, and they are devoted to analysis. In the transference the analyst is treated as a pleasant, appreciative parent surrogate. The patients' underlying sexuality and hostility is disguised by a façade of cooperativeness, interest, and analytic adeptness. The oedipal form of the transference is powerfully defended against, and when it is brought to the attention of these patients, they become anxious and depressed. The analysis stops running so smoothly.

Sheila Gray

Ekstein suggests that playing and dreaming are intimately connected. Just as one may consider a child's play to be his or her major form of dreaming, one may consider an adult's dream his or her major form of playing with thoughts. Both have as their aim the resolution of inner conflict. The dreams of the child, which seem to reflect developmental lines quite accurately, also resemble fairy tales in their symbolic form and in their functions as wish-fulfillments, as ways to resolve inner conflicts and developmental dilemmas, and as ways of performing developmental tasks. Thus, analysis of children's dreams leads equally to understanding of the child's unconscious mental life and of his developmental reality.

International Journal of Group Psychotherapy. XXIX, 1979

Therapeutic Groups for the Children of Holocaust Survivors. E. Fogelman and Bella Savran. Pp. 211-235.

Geraldine Pederson-Krag

Geraldine Pederson-Krag

Geraldine Pederson-Krag  

Children of the Holocaust survivors bear some of the pain and problems of their parents' lives. They need sympathetic listeners with the patience and stamina to appreciate the horrors they hear and the feelings these horrors evoke in the narrator. The survivors themselves are uncertain whether they should retell memories or repress them. There seems to be no opportunity for the children to discuss their fears, so they have lived alone with fantasies, secrets, and confusions. A quarter of a million children of survivors live in the United States but they have only recently begun to share their feelings publicly.

The authors, themselves children of survivors, formed nine therapeutic groups, balanced by sex and age, in which participants could share their thoughts and feelings and through support decrease their sense of isolation and improve their self-images. The groups were essentially discussion groups, traditional psychotherapy groups, or therapeutically oriented awareness groups. The pregroup interview was all-important; applicants were asked to describe succinctly their current life, their past, the lives of their parents, the ways in which the parents dealt with the Holocaust experience as the children were growing up, and how the applicants themselves dealt with the experience. Some responded in unemotional, intellectualized ways, others with intense outbursts. They were encouraged to express anxieties, questions, or fears during the initial interview. Where possible, applicants were grouped according to social, political, religious, and geographical backgrounds. Participants agreed to attend all eight sessions, to be honest and open, and not to identify members of the group to outsiders. Transference was not discussed because of the time limit.

Winnicott was concerned with the infant's struggle to make the transition from a world of total subjectivity to a world in which objective events are subject to differences and are acknowledged to have a significance of their own. International Journal of Group Psychotherapy. XXX, 1980

A Modified Group Treatment for Elderly Narcissistic Patients. Brian E. Levine and Marcia Poston. Pp. 153-167.

Geraldine Pederson-Krag

Geraldine Pederson-Krag

Geraldine Pederson-Krag  

Elderly chronic complainers lacking insight and potential for change are traditionally seen in individual sessions which turn out to be unproductive and frustrating. They tend to be depressed by loss of the self-esteem that arises from usefulness and by physical and mental deterioration. Such depression is often manifested as physical complaints. With little observing ego, such patients come to the clinic unaware of the impact of their behavior on others. Comments from the therapist on their behavior are felt as narcissistic assaults. It was hoped that the presence of other patients in a group would make these comments less threatening. Yet a group of patients treated in a conventional manner tended to talk simultaneously, their only object a description of their symptoms. There was rivalry for the attention of the therapist. The patients met for a half hour of refreshments and informal spontaneous discussion before getting together for supervised talk. In the more formal second session patients were better able to wait their turn and to talk about matters with greater relevance and emotional meaning. The therapists in a nurturing role were able to show interest in the patients' immediate concerns.

John Ross  

DISCUSSION: Dr. Martin Blum echoed the classical analyst's questioning whether the new self psychology is the "wave of the future" and cautioned against the reductionism, scholasticism, and schisms which have periodically plagued psychoanalysis. Dr. Blum implied, however, that traditionalists may be similarly culpable, especially to the extent that they concentrate on theory to the exclusion of practice. There is merit in Kohut, particularly the Kohut of the 1965 Freud Anniversary Lecture, which was an extension of Maxwell Gitelson's paper, "The Curative Factors in Psychoanalysis." Gitelson had concentrated on the first phase of analysis, before the emergence of the working alliance and the transference neurosis proper. This was characterized by a "beginning ego change" resulting from identification with the analyst and the establishment of those dyadic conditions under which narcissism can give way to object love. Rapport, like empathy, is crucial during this initial period. Dr. Blum noted that such a concept contrasts with Dr. Charles Brenner's positing of a single attitude, the interpretive stance, as predominating throughout treatment. Instead, it asserts that transference is itself a developmental milestone, easily jeopardized by insensitive, premature interpretation or aloofness. As far back as Abraham it was recognized that narcissistic patients must be "gotten past" the "first phase of analysis.

October 28, 1980. THE UBIQUITOUS PRIMAL DEFENSIVE MECHANISMS. Andrew Peto, M.D.

Dr. Peto postulated the following as the specific causal mechanism in depression or depressive affect: "The aggressive cathexes operating through the ego are directed from a very specific representation against another very specific representation. This representation is always part of the self or part of the object representation. Correspondingly, it is either only part of the ego aggressively functioning against another part of the ego, or it is only part of the superego aggressively functioning against part of the ego." In disagreement with Dr. Charles Brenner's view on the genesis of affects in general and depressive affect in particular, Dr. Peto suggested that depression can manifest itself before it is associated with a definite idea, provided the above mechanism is present. Dr. Peto prefers the term mechanism to the term conflict because he is referring to a time in life when the child's cognitive function does not distinguish between self and non-self. Charakter Und Neurose. Ansätze Zu Einer Psychoanalytischen Charakterologie. (Character and Neurosis. Starting Points for a Psychoanalytic Characterology.)

By S. O. Hoffmann. Frankfurt am Main: Suhrkamp Verlag, 1979. 358 pp.

Ernest Wolf

Ernest Wolf

Ernest S. Wolf
CHICAGO

Ernest Wolf  

The modest subtitle of this scholarly monograph disguises a serious and largely successful attempt to provide a comprehensive survey of the development and nature of the concept of character in psychoanalysis. To this encyclopedic enterprise the author adds his own point of view, which is conservative and traditional in the face of the controversies springing from postclassical revisions of Freudian theory. At the same time, the monograph contains a presentation, albeit often summarized all too briefly, of views with which the author is not in sympathy.

The book is divided into an introduction and four parts, with Part One and Part Two providing the bulk of the material.

In his introduction, Hoffmann sets the tone of the book as he discusses his preference for the term "character" over that of "personality." Perhaps not unexpectedly, he is partial to the German language tradition of the term "character," which he feels to be the more dynamic one, even though it is a borrowed word. The term "personality," which he estimates to be more commonly in use in Anglo-American literature, he judges to be less psychoanalytic, more descriptive, and to deal more with traits, patterns, and behavior. Clearly, the two overlap and the differences are subtle, although they are unmistakable to a psychoanalyst. This is a sophisticated book that acknowledges the impossibility of giving clear, precise, well-defined answers while it constructively pursues the possibility of approaching the elusive and almost unknowable. It does this simultaneously from different directions, with a resulting movement toward the "truth" that derives strength from a dialectical process which includes even so-called unacceptable options.

Part One consists of an attempt to reach a definition of the term character as it is used in psychoanalysis. Attention is paid to its differentiation from such related concepts as structure, neurotic character, character neurosis, and psychopathy. By Arthur H. Green, M.D. London/New York: Aronson, 1980. 314 pp.

Lawrence Shaderowfsky

Lawrence Shaderowfsky

Lawrence Shaderowfsky
NEW YORK

Lawrence Shaderowfsky  

This book describes the various ways in which children have suffered physical and sexual abuse and neglect at the hands of their parents and caretakers. It is a handbook for all workers in the mental health field. It outlines the contributory factors, the treatment modalities available, and the social institutions involved.

The number of victims, at least in the hundreds of thousands in this country annually, is shocking. The group that Green has studied comes from the lowest socioeconomic minority stratum. This is the most visible group. Here ignorance, poverty, and familial instability are major contributory factors. The inevitable involvement of a variety of social agencies has brought to light an area which once was the exclusive and private domain of parents. The sectors of the population which are not subject to such public scrutiny, the middle and upper classes, are the principal source of our private patients. Our clinical experience with adult patients occasionally reveals the kind of mistreatment described by Green, with the patient himself either as abuser or as someone who was abused as a child. When children become our patients, the frequency of serious maltreatment becomes even more evident.

In his description of the contributing factors, Green cites social stresses and internalized parental psychopathology.

Revue Française De Psychanalyse. XLII, 1978

Oedipus on Cithaeron. Claude Le Guen. Pp. 19-37.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

The author reviews a thesis he developed in his book, The Original Oedipus. Le Guen is dissatisfied both with Freud's phylogenetic speculations concerning the primal horde and with Melanie Klein's ultraprecocious ego and object with an equally precocious oedipal situation. The Kleinian view is even more obscurantist, he feels, than Freud's anthropological speculations. Psychoanalysis furnishes the means to analyze myths, but should not itself rest on a myth. However, if the Freudian and Kleinan mythologies concerning the origin of the oedipus complex are put aside, the question of origins remains to be answered. For Le Guen, the problem is more epistemological than historical. Whatever is said about the first days, weeks, and months of life must always remain purely speculative, because the only arguments available rest on assumptions and cannot be criticized. In his book Le Guen suggested the advent of stranger anxiety as a central moment in the development of the psyche. At this moment the nuclear perception of mother and not-mother begins, a triangular relationship is established, and the maternal object is constituted only with the aid of a third object, the intruding father. The infant's perception of the nonidentity of the stranger with the mother comes to signal to the infant the possibility of the absence of the mother. It is this experience of the loss of the primary object which makes that primary object come to exist for the infant as separate. At the same moment the infant experiences himself as an individual separate from the primary object. The stranger, however, is not invested as an object, but is only the signifier of the possible loss of mother. This "negation of a presence and affirmation of an absence" is called by Le Guen the "not-mother." Thus there develops the first pair of opposites (mother/not-mother) in what is actually a triadic relationship. Le Guen concludes from this that no relationship is ever actually dual. The subject does not come into existence until situated from the very beginning in a conflictual triangular relationship. In this, Le Guen believes he has discovered the original model of the oedipus complex, establishing, organizing, and anticipating all subsequent developmental evolution. The second triadic relationship, the classical oedipal complex discussed by Freud, occurs when the father replaces the not-mother and becomes an individualized object with which the child may identify. This manner of viewing the oedipal conflict permits a rethinking of the developmental process. Le Guen's is a new theoretical concept, a reductive move (as all theoretical conceptualizations are an attempt to reduce the complexity of experience). The important issues thus become questions of the concept's value in terms of the rest of the theory and its clinical implications.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

This paper develops a theme of Winnicott's on the use a patient allows himself to make of the analyst. Potamianou suggests that some patients enter analysis just at the time they are working on some aspects of the process of separation from parents. Such patients use the analyst as a symbol of the reunion with the mother in a mother-child dyad. These efforts toward separation involve a setting in motion of some rather violent instinctual impulses which are as yet unintegrated. While the process of achieving autonomy and the affirmation of identity are aided by the analysis, these patients use the analyst only for a while and tend to leave analysis prematurely. The author reviews some cases in her experience and suggests that the function of the analyst in such clinical situations is different from Winnicott's concept of holding. Instead, the analyst must be someone "who can let go." The complex countertransferential aspects of such a task are discussed.

Color and Creativity. Some Reflections on the Work of Odilon Redon. Janine Cophignon. Pp. 215-251.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

The French painter and etcher, Odilon Redon, a visionary and a precursor of the surrealists, spent the major part of his artistic career working only with black and white media. Only late in his development did he come to utilize color in his work, producing, for example, delicate and sensitive pastel renderings of floral bouquets. The author's work with two artistic patients with conflicts about color tempts her to take a psychoanalytic approach to this evolution in Redon from sombre black and white to an extraordinary sensitivity to color. In both of her analytic cases, the inhibition concerning color depended on unconscious wishes concerning death, violence, and rage which had not been integrated. In both cases, the experience of fusion was particularly important and involved many themes such as the double and the mirror.

Revue Française De Psychanalyse. XLII, 1978

What I Understand by and about Primary Repression. Ilana Schimmel. Pp. 479-498.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

The concept of primary repression is an important but controversial aspect of Freudian theory. It is a thesis which Freud maintained even after the introduction of the structural hypothesis, according to Schimmel. Primary repression derives from an irreducible instinctual conflict and is a universal mechanism which is constitutive of the unconscious. This repression becomes repression proper (in our usual sense of selective and dynamic forgetting) only when attached to representations. Yet the concept of primary repression raises many problems. Schimmel focuses on the energic aspects, to which she believes topographical, structural, and dynamic considerations are subordinate in Freud's discussion of primary repression. She raises two central problems. The first is concerned with the relationship between representations and energy, how this linkage comes about, and how it comes to play a determining role in the development of repression. The second problem concerns the manner in which primary repression comes about when the repressing structure, the ego, does not yet exist. Schimmel argues for a diachronic view, a linear historical perspective on the development of the psychic apparatus.

Revue Française De Psychanalyse. XLII, 1978

Borderline Organization and Psychotic Conditions. Giovanni Hautmann. Pp. 775-875.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

In this lengthy study the author presents a theory of the formation of the self and discusses the role of symbol-formation and narcissism. He attempts to link his theory to clinical material relating to borderline and psychotic patients. The central thesis of the paper is that in psychosis there exists a deficit in the process of symbolization, which permits the retention of asymbolic elements in the psyche. These asymbolic aspects interfere with normal functioning of the self and with the acquisition of a capacity for the mastery of stress. Hautmann reviews Freud's comments on the development of symbolic systems and the development of Freud's thought on the relationship between the symbolic system and psychosis. Repression, repudiation, denial, and splitting of the ego are stages in the development of Freud's reflections on the specific psychotic defense. Hautmann emphasizes that the essential element in splitting is that the symbolic system has not been able to become organized; he also stresses that Freud thought of perception as an active process. He infers that the self organizes itself by forming a layer of thought processes which elaborates each given of psychical reality by inscription in a symbolic system. One of the functions of this symbolization is the organization of a within and a without, that is, the development of a dimensional aspect to the psychic apparatus. This can be linked to incorporation and expulsion and to affirmation and negation. In psychotics this demarcation of without and within fails. Hautmann introduces case material from borderline and prepsychotic patients.

Psyche. XXXIV, 1980

Freud—a Structuralist? Hermann Lang. Pp. 865-884.

In their methodological development the French structuralists lay claim to Freud as their sponsor. Such a postulate is a paradox, in that the structuralist "super-rationalism" seeks particularly to understand that domain which Freud, using the terms "unconscious" and "id," had characterized as instinctive and irrational. According to Jacques Lacan, this concept is comprised in the following well-known dictum: "The unconscious is structured like a language." In interpreting the works of Freud, Lang seeks to find concepts which could legitimate this pronouncement and which could also offer more possibilities for convergence—for example in the idea of the "devaluation of the conscious Ego.

Psyche. XXXIV, 1980

The Dialectic in Freud's Concept of Consciousness. Reinhold Bianchi. Pp. 977-996.

Bianchi points out that two concepts of consciousness are found in Freud's writings. Metapsychology is concerned with the critique of neurotic, "false" consciousness, which is blind to its entanglement with drives. In the technical writings and in the discussion of therapeutic goals, the concern is with a broadened, "authentic" consciousness.

Eckstaedt reconstructs painter Paul Klee's artistic mastery of the oedipal conflict situation on the basis of one of his early drawings. Thanks to his talent, the boy succeeded, by means of graphic construction and self-representation, in playfully sublimating his oedipal desire for his mother and his wish to eliminate his male rival. In this way he approached the solution of his drive conflict.

Meeting of the Psychoanalytic Institute of New England, East

October 26, 1981. PSYCHOANALYTIC OBSERVATIONS ON THE PREDICTION OF PHYSICAL ILLNESS. Samuel Silverman, M.D.

Dr. Silverman emphasized the need for an approach to the prediction and prevention of physical illness that would include psychological predictors. He referred to the 1923 work of Scholz and Pfeiffer who reported that "nervousness" preceded the diagnosis of cancer of the tail of the pancreas. After World War II, recognition of the role of emotion in physical illness increased. The emphasis was on the etiological aspects, and, unfortunately, the trend was toward the "packaging of personality traits and assigning them to a particular somatic disease—a simplistic and superficial approach."

Dr. Silverman's data were derived from studies of patients seen in extensive consultation or therapy (mostly psychoanalysis) to evaluate the predictive aspects of psychological factors. He considers psychological stress and its often unrecognized unconscious significance as a necessary but insufficient predictor of physical illness. He found that the "psychological matrix" of these patients contained a number of different predictors: heredity, somatic identification, insufficiency of psychological homeostatic mechanisms, transference manifestations, and dreams. They are important in determining the type of response to stress, including the possibility of physical illness. Dr. Silverman gave clinical examples illustrating each predictor but cautioned that these cases should not be seen as demonstrating a review of all such signals.

Heredity is important in any psychological "risk-profile." It may indicate which organ system will be involved. For example, a patient with a strong family history of glaucoma presented with a competitive struggle which involved his father. Upon winning, he developed a corneal inflammation. He also revealed intense guilt over his hostility.

The process of "somatic identification" may point to the organ system which will malfunction. Somatic identification is linked with essentially preoedipal conflicts about a key object in which deneutralized aggression, intensive guilt, and need for atonement are involved.

DISCUSSION: Dr. Cornelis Heijn, Jr., presented a case of a thirty-eight-year-old woman who developed a life-threatening ventricular arrythmia upon attempting to mail a letter that would take her away from her mother. Since she was away from her father when he died, the letter was, in primary process terms, her mother's death warrant. Dr. Heijn agreed with Dr. Silverman's basic premises, although he expressed the wish for some clarification of aspects of the paper. "Is stress always present before physical illness, or is Dr. Silverman implying it is a necessary but not sufficient condition?" He also wondered about the prospective nature of Dr. Silverman's predictors. Were these discovered upon reviewing the clinical data? Dr. Heijn then focused on the need for verification of Dr. Silverman's hypotheses. He proposed the following basic requirements: (1) "definitions need to be operationalized"; (2) "data would need to be adequate"; and (3) "the full data needs to be evaluated by neutral observers of equal sophistication." When validation becomes more effective, we, and medicine in general, will be able to rely on Dr. Silverman's findings more fully. Dr.
