[[RunningHead]]

Contemporary Psychoanalysis. XVII, 1981

Unconscious Wishes and Human Relationships. Joseph Sandler. Pp. 180-196.

Ronald Krasner

Ronald Krasner

Ronald Krasner  

Sandler attempts in this paper to resolve the unnecessary conflict and the gap which he perceives to exist between drive theory and object relations theory. The unconscious wish/fantasy is explored as a way of approaching this problem. Sandler achieves resolution through a definition of terms by stating "that every wish comes to include a representation of the person's own self and a representation of the object…" He states that not all wishes are motivated only by sexual or aggressive drives, but primarily by attempts to maintain well-being and security. As a result, a psychology based on drive discharge should be replaced by a psychoanalytic psychology related to the control of feeling states. Sandler suggests that Freud's concept of an "identity of perception," i.e., the attainment of satisfaction through the re-experiencing of a memory, is an alternative to wish-fulfillment through drive discharge. Illusional actualization, delusional actualization, hallucinatory actualization, and actualization through daydreams are the mechanisms of this wish-fulfillment. It is the motivational force of feeling safe that Sandler feels bridges the gap between the two theories.

481

Developmental Vicissitudes, Object Relations, and Psychopathology. Peter L. Giovacchini. Pp. 258-275.

Ronald Krasner

Ronald Krasner

Ronald Krasner  

To highlight his developmental/object relations frame of reference, Giovacchini, at the beginning of this paper, demonstrates the polemic between those analysts who continue to believe in the death instinct versus those who are devoted to the centrality of the oedipus complex. His point of view has caused controversy and attack from "orthodox" psychoanalysts. After defining psychoanalysis and its methodology and stating that the only principle essential to it is psychic determinism, he introduces the concept of a prementational level of development. This concept is illustrated in two clinical vignettes. In the discussion he elaborates on a scheme of development wherein there is a prementational phase dominated by circadian rhythms, followed by a presymbiotic phase, then symbiotic fusion, then the establishment of part objects, and finally, well-structured object relations. While acknowledging that his theorizing is subject to a good deal of "adultomorphization," he presents a new idea that during the transitional phase, not only objects, but also nurturing functions may be subject to blurred boundaries. A further explanation of the prementational phase, including the postulation of a "nurturing matrix," is undertaken, leading to Giovacchini's speculation that the borderline pathology which was evident in the clinical material presented can be understood in terms of disturbances in the development of this nurturing matrix.

482

The case of Frau Emmy von N. is re-examined from the perspective of the author's own theory of the paranoid process. Meissner's thesis is that the memories of traumatic events uncovered by Freud through hypnosis may not have been the etiologic factors in Frau Emmy's disorder, but may instead have been memories which had been preserved and organized by the patient to reinforce and sustain an already existing sense of herself as a victim, itself an expression of her pathological narcissism.

The Problem of Infantile Omnipotence. Helen R. Beiser. Pp. 113-131.

Melvin Stanger

Melvin Stanger

Melvin Stanger  

In this interesting and provocative article, Beiser attempts to differentiate between infantile omnipotence which is a part of ongoing normal development and various forms of pathological omnipotence which may occur secondarily. this is done by tracing infantile omnipotence and its vicissitudes as a developmental thread throughout the life span of the individual. There follows a discussion of the importance of infantile impotence in the clinical psychoanalytic setting, beginning with the fantasy of the power of the analyst or of the psychoanalytic setting itself and going on to the various transference manifestations in which omnipotence may play a role. Beiser makes a useful point that some patients may need to separate from their powerful analysts in the latter part of their analyses by talking about various events and new activities outside the analyst's office, and that this should not be interpreted as a transference resistance.

This is a fascinating and moving account of the analysis of a woman in her late twenties whose father had a stroke when she was nine, after which he became bedridden and deteriorated. He finally died during the middle of the patient's analysis. From the clinical material the author convincingly demonstrates how the analyst, through the transference, became a substitute object through whom the previously impeded mourning became possible.

Screen Memories as Transference Resistance. Gordon F. Lewis. Pp. 159-170.

Melvin Stanger

Melvin Stanger  

The author of this well-written paper, after exploring the origins of the concept of screen memories, traces its evolution in the analytic literature. This involves a further understanding of the various ways in which screen memories, including traumatic memories, may serve as resistances. Thus the author arrives at a more comprehensive definition of screen memories. Finally, he presents some instructive case material from a psychoanalysis, demonstrating how screen memories can be acted out in the service of the transference resistance and how it is then necessary, at the appropriate time, to interpret the screen memory directly into the transference as wish or as defense.

Narcissistic Personality and Borderline Conditions: a Differential Diagnosis. W. W. Meissner. Pp. 171-202.

Melvin Stanger

Melvin Stanger

Melvin Stanger  

In a thorough and well-reasoned set of propositions Meissner attempts a more definitive differentiation than has yet been made between narcissistic personality and borderline conditions. He differentiates the two groups according to the kinds of transferences they form and according to the stability and cohesiveness of the sense of self that they manifest. More important, he attempts a detailed structural differentiation between the two groups involving their differing introjective organizations. Meissner shows that the narcissistic personality has not been as much contaminated by aggressive derivatives, while the borderline person has been unable to integrate the hostile and loving parts of the parental imago because of the unresolved aggressive components stemming from deviant resolutions of the rapprochement crisis. This is because "the narcissistic child does not meet the same degree of parental rejection, disapproval, hostility or destructiveness" as the borderline child does during separation-individuation. Instead "the [narcissistic child's] problem … concerns the loss, potential or actual, of the narcissistic availability of the parent, as separation and the establishment of autonomy assert themselves.

The Interpretation of Dreams and Infantile Cerebral Paralysis: Remarks on Freud's Theorization. Heinz G. Schott. Pp. 97-110.

Freud's 1897 treatise on infantile cerebral paralysis, based on clinical observation, and his Interpretation of Dreams, based on psychological self-observation, are compared in order to gain insight into the development of Freud's theory. It is apparent that the concept of a more highly developed system suppressing a more primitive one (and the possibility of an eruption of the suppressed system) played an important role even in Freud's prepsychological writings, as did the concept of muscular and ideational work.

Revue Française De Psychanalyse. XLI, 1977

For the Fiftieth Anniversary Issue of the Revue. Janine Chasseguet-Smirgel. Pp. 415-428.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

Chasseguet-Smirgel stresses the links between the Parisian Psychoanalytic Society and the Revue, both of which were celebrating their fiftieth anniversaries in 1977. She discusses the early history of psychoanalysis in France, evoking the literary and artistic ambience of the 1920's in Paris at the time that initial psychoanalytic efforts were being carried out in France. Translations into French, however, were late in appearing: The Interpretation of Dreams was not translated until 1926. The impetus for the early analytic developments came largely from French-speaking Swiss analysts. An early worker was Mme. Eugénie Sokolnicka, a lay analyst who was herself analyzed by Jung, by Freud, and later by Ferenczi. She in turn analyzed two founding members of the Parisian analytic group, Edouard Pichon and René Laforgue. The author traces the founding of the Parisian analytic society and the roles played by René Laforgue and Marie Bonaparte. The Society was founded in 1926, with ten members, including Laforgue, Pichon, Loewenstein, and Raymond de Saussure. The first conference of French-speaking analysts took place in August 1926, and the Revue made its appearance in 1927. This article includes brief biographies of many of these founding figures, as well as an account of the early years of the Society, its development during the 1930's, the activities which were still carried on to some extent during the Occupation, the "boom" in psychoanalysis after the war, the growth of the Society, and the subsequent schisms.

Art and Syndrome. Francis Pasche. Pp. 465-480.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

Pasche questions the current tendency to degrade artistic creativity by considering it a symptom. He sees this as a reductive tendency, abandoning the uniqueness of artistic efforts in favor of the view that such productions are on the level of any other human striving. For Pasche, there are many contemporary reductive tendencies: structuralist, political, and psychoanalytic. This demythification of creative genius is simply a particular case of the negation of values in general. In contrast, he holds that the psychoanalytic approach to art reveals the limitations of applied analysis. Artistic activity is not a symptom, whatever the analogies one might find between the genesis of art and the manifestations of hysteria or delusions. One would look in vain for the essence of a work of art in the unconscious intrigue brought to light by analysts.

Heinz Kohut—1913-1981

George Pollock

George Pollock

George Pollock  

Heinz Kohut died in Chicago on October 8, 1981, at the age of sixty-eight. I had known Heinz for more than thirty years. He was one of my teachers at the Chicago Institute, he was my friend, my colleague, and a courageous man who was respected, highly regarded, and a charismatic figure to many.

In recent years, his theoretical and clinical ideas stimulated new lines of thought, controversy, and ferment. His ideas provided additional evidence that in our field not all psychoanalysts agree with one another, and ours is not a set of clinical theories that are immutable. In fact, our discipline has a history that is filled with debate and disagreements. It is this level of skepticism that can be very fruitful for further advances. Theories are evaluated by clinicians and scholars on the basis of evidence. Through this process of scientific assessment, theories are modified, accepted, questioned, rejected, or may become the stimulus for further scientific research. Unfortunately, issues of politics, prejudice, power, and ad hominem concerns can interfere with the more objective evaluation of the ideas. If a field is to grow and develop, we must pay attention to newer concepts and not become too involved with the people who are identified with the ideas themselves. This observation is not new, but I feel it bears repetition if we are to assess a contribution, whether it proves to be all or partially correct or incorrect, independent of the originators.

The facts of Heinz's life are known: his migration to the United States in wartime as a result of Hitler's anti-Semitism and racial laws; his arrival in Chicago, alone and without close friends or family; his progression through neurology to psychiatry and psychoanalysis. His encouragement of younger people may be less known. I first met Heinz through his writings.

284

Crises and Special Problems in Psychoanalysis and Psychotherapy

By Leopold Bellak, M.D. with Peri Faithorn, M.D. New York: Brunner/Mazel, 1981. 249 pp.

Samuel Hoch

Samuel Hoch

Samuel Hoch
SAN FRANCISCO

Samuel Hoch  

Rather than classify this volume as a technical work, which may have been the author's primary intent, it can better be regarded as a collection of tactics or, as is described in the introductory pages, as containing an assortment of "suggested stratagems" for managing unusual situations that bedevil patients and therapists alike. The latter include suicidal danger, psychosis, major surgery, pregnancy, and divorce. Attention is directed not only to certain problems in the "ordinary psychotherapeutic situation," but especially to patients with more difficult disorders. Flexibility is vigorously promoted as therapists are urged to tailor the therapeutic process to special needs. The book is oriented toward clinicians interested mainly in psychoanalytic psychotherapy (including psychoanalysis proper). A cogent argument can be made, however, that Bellak's recommendations are often likely to preclude the very process he seeks to preserve and render more efficient.

Bellak emphasizes the importance of therapeutic neutrality and interpretation and recommends that one abandon neutrality only in "special circumstances." He takes this position in his introduction and then leaves no doubt about the dangers and damage he believes are created by therapeutic rigidity. Few experienced clinicians would disagree with him. But he gives insufficient attention to the cautious reservations psychoanalysts have about departing from standard technique, and serious questions can be raised about the techniques Bellak recommends in this book.

The goals and functioning of the Hampstead Nursery School for the Blind are demonstrated through the use of detailed descriptions of how different blind children interact with staff and with other blind children. The staff fosters and utilizes optimal auditory, tactile, and olfactory stimulation to enhance reality testing, cognitive development, and personal relations. An essential staff task is to help the mothers with their many problems; e.g., denial of the child's visual impairment, intolerance of the problem, and inability to talk to the child about his/her blindness.

The development of speech and its precursors is compared in seeing and blind children. The author provides a detailed description of two blind children who eventually achieved normal speech. A healthy mother-child interaction throughout infancy is essential for optimal speech and cognitive development in the seeing child; it is even more important for the blind. The highest priority should

329

therefore be given to providing the mother with the help she needs, notably early treatment of the depression commonly seen in mothers of blind (and other handicapped) children.

Data from the analyses of two women clarify some of the ways in which disturbances in separation and individuation produce or aggravate later psychopathology. The data also demonstrate that the often critical events of the preverbal years are more accessible to psychoanalytic investigation in the treatment of adults than has heretofore been assumed. Patients whose preverbal development has been impaired tend to reveal frequent body manifestations of conflict, and they tend to have florid physical complaints more often than other patients.

Freud. The Man and the Cause

By Ronald W. Clark. New York: Random House, 1980. 652 pp.

Henry Lowenfeld

Henry Lowenfeld

Henry Lowenfeld
NEW YORK

Henry Lowenfeld  

The author, Ronald W. Clark, born and living in England, is well known for his biographies of great men—Einstein, Bertrand Russell, and others—of the twentieth century. His books have been popular and successful.

Since Jones wrote his official biography, Clark states, a great deal of new material about Freud's life has been published. In this new biography of Freud, Clark has drawn upon a wealth of Freud's letters that have become available. Particularly rewarding is Clark's consideration of Freud's youthful letters to his young friends, Fluss and Silberstein. These letters show Freud as an adolescent in a state of passionate and enthusiastic creativity. This period in Freud's life appears quite typical for gifted young boys of that era. Freud does not look very different from his friends who in later life went on to very ordinary achievements.

A strange story, based on Renée Gicklhorn's research, concerns the report of a second wife of Freud's father, Jacob, registered by the Catholic authorities as Rebecca Freud. Another document is quoted to the effect that she came to Freiberg with his two sons. There is no other evidence of Rebecca, so that the story is very hard to believe. Clark hesitates to come to a definite conclusion, however, since it is also hard to believe that bureaucrats would invent a wife. Clark points out that if there had been another stepmother for the two sons before Sigmund Freud's mother became Jacob Freud's wife, the family experience in Freud's childhood would have been even more complex and confusing than our evidence heretofore has indicated.

Another interesting item concerns Freud's Uncle Joseph. In The Interpretation of Dreams Freud mentioned that this uncle had gotten into trouble with the law and that his father was so shaken by the experience that his hair turned grey within a few days.

[[RunningHead]]

Psyche and Society. Explorations in Psychoanalytic Sociology

By Robert Endleman. New York: Columbia University Press, 1981. 465 pp.

Aaron Esman

Aaron Esman

Aaron H. Esman
NEW YORK

Aaron Esman  

For decades interested parties have sought, with indifferent success, to arrange a marriage between psychoanalysis and the social sciences. The difficulty, as Robert Endleman, a psychoanalytically trained sociologist, explains in this rather curious book, has been either the pretension of each discipline to "imperialism," in which it seeks to impose its frame of reference on the other, or "separation," in which each has insisted on the purity and immiscibility of its own doctrines. Endleman's stated aim is to arrive at an "integrationist" position whose fundamental propositions are these:

1. Any social science requires an underlying psychology of the individual human being, essentially a psychology of the nature of human nature, and

2. Any adequate psychology of human beings also requires an understanding of social processes and of the patterns and processes of culture and how these in turn affect the individual human personality (p. 15).

Illustrative examples of such "integrationists" are anthropologists Róheim, La Barre, Devereux, Anne Parsons, and Muensterberger (whom Endleman erroneously describes as a non-clinician).

In pursuit of his own effort at "integration," Endleman attempts no less than an explanatory account of human evolution, drawing from a wide range of sources in paleontology and evolutionary biology as well as from his own chosen fields to account, more or less plausibly, for the evolutionary emergence of such human characteristics as bipedal locomotion, language, the frontal coital position, the oedipus complex, and the incest taboo. He emerges, in his own terms, with a rewritten Totem and Taboo, devoid of Freud's Lamarckianism and resting instead on Róheim's concepts of cultural origins and intergenerational transmission. This reviewer is not competent to assess the sociological data, but Endleman does appear to be knowing and effective in his application of psychoanalytic concepts and developmental theory. One can question some of his formulations and syntheses—particularly his account of the frontal coital position as a return to the primal nursing posture—but his ideas are challenging and his scholarship is impressive.

The Fate of the Unconscious in the Human Sciences

Yiannis Gabriel

Yiannis Gabriel

Yiannis Gabriel
27 Poplar Grove
London W6 TRF
England

Yiannis Gabriel  

ABSTRACT

In this essay the author seeks to answer some of the criticisms of Freud's central concepts, theories, and methods that have been raised by twentieth century philosophy. He argues that many of these concepts and theories, particularly the concept of the unconscious, represent indispensable assumptions shared by the human sciences, even when they are not directly addressed by them. Further, he argues that in Freud's ideas we find one of the most advanced positions in our understanding of culture, its illusions and discontents, and a profound attempt to bridge the distance between a description of social reality and its critical appraisal.

Child Analysis and Therapy

Edited by Jules Glenn, M.D. with the assistance of Melvin A. Scharfman, M.D. New York: Jason Aronson, Inc., 1978. 759 pp.

Samuel Ritvo

Samuel Ritvo

Samuel Ritvo
NEW HAVEN, CONN.

Samuel Ritvo  

This book was originally to have been part of an encyclopedia of psychoanalysis. When the encyclopedia project was abandoned, the authors who had agreed to contribute articles on child analysis decided to produce this independent volume consisting of twenty-five chapters by twenty-nine distinguished authors in the fields of child analysis, child psychotherapy, child development, early childhood education, and special education. The volume is organized into eight parts. After an introductory overview of child analytic technique and a section on general principles of child analysis by the editor, there are sections on: assessment of patients for child analysis; child analysis at different developmental stages; specific aspects of the analytic process, such as the opening phase, transference and the transference neurosis, dream analysis, and termination; adjuncts to child analysis, e.g., tutoring and nursery school; the analysis of adopted children as a special situation; and a final section on the applications of the principles of child analysis to prevention, diagnostic evaluation, child psychotherapy, and the psychotherapy of psychotic children.

The organization of the volume, with its thorough, rational, encyclopedic approach, is one of its strengths. At the same time this contributes to one of the drawbacks because a number of the writers start with a statement of the principles of child analysis as they apply to that topic; consequently there is considerable repetition. However, every major topic in child analysis and therapy is covered by psychoanalytic clinicians rich in experience who distill their experience and share it with the reader. This they do in two main ways: by formulating their ideas and principles in a common theoretical framework which gives the volume a unity that could not otherwise have been achieved; and by illustrating their formulations generously with case material which in a number of instances is quite extensively presented, yet focused by the topic of the chapter. This makes the book useful for student and teacher alike, as we always feel the need for more published case reports.

Certain Aspects of Narcissism. Robert Mirouze. Pp. 65-88.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

Mirouze discusses his treatment of an erythrophobic patient for whom the classical explanations of erythrophobia were not helpful. The theoretical work of Kohut was, in contrast, very important in Mirouze's understanding and analytic efforts with this patient. The classical view of blushing considers it to be genital excitation which undergoes an exhibitionistic regression and a displacement to the face. The syndrome is thus regarded as an aspect of anxiety hysteria, with shame linked to oedipal guilt. For Mirouze's patient, however, it seemed more appropriate to consider the phobic symptom related to the shame of narcissistic injury. Shame was utilized as a danger-signal which permitted the ego to institute a flight, that is, a rejection of an object relation, in favor of maintaining the cohesion of the grandiose self. Exhibitionistic and omnipotent tendencies could not risk being disavowed by an environment which did not conform to and support the patient's narcissism. Mirouze reviews the progress of the case, noting that the patient steadily improved when interpretations were given within the framework provided by Kohut. He uses this case presentation to discuss Kohut's theories and to criticize some of Kernberg's. Concluding that Kohut's theories have a practical value and applicability for clinicians, he finds this especially interesting, in that Kohut's work developed within a metapsychological framework not in vogue in French theoretical circles and held suspect by them. He questions whether, because French theorists express justifiable criticisms of Hartmann's ego psychology, they should reject all elaborations of it concerning the notion of the self. He feels that Kohut's work should be given careful consideration.

Fragments of the History of Epilepsy. Therèse Neyraut-Sutterman. Pp. 439-478.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

Neyraut-Sutterman approaches the study of epilepsy through her work with an analytic patient whose central unconscious fantasy was an incestuous return to his mother's womb. This seemed to corroborate Ferenczi's view of the unconscious meaning of epileptic seizures. The author reviews recent neurological and psychoanalytic work on epilepsy, but is interested also in mythological material surrounding epilepsy. She relies heavily on a recent work by G. Dumenzil, Myth and Epic, whose interpretation of the Hercules myth suggests a kinship with other folk heroes whose "functional sins" involved transgressions against deity, against the role of warrior, and against sexual taboos. Neyraut-Sutterman attempts a psychoanalytic interpretation of this ancient myth of epilepsy. She takes note of the continuing controversies surrounding theories of epilepsy and suggests that each scientific system of thought has a need to revise and fix the place of epilepsy in that system. Epilepsy is therefore something like the umbilicus of various enigmas, especially the mind-body problem.

670

The Presence of the Third Party in Psychoanalysis: The Problem of Payment by Others. Johannes Cremerius. Pp. 1-41.

For several years a conflict has been smoldering between those who favor psychoanalytic treatment financed by medical insurance plans and those who oppose this arrangement on the ground that it is incompatible with the therapeutic goals of psychoanalysis. In discussing this conflict, the author comes to the conclusion that "pure" analysis, as conceived by Freud, is a normative concept which is continually negated by the reality of psychoanalytic treatment. The

674

steady presence of third parties in analysis—the presence of society and of social norms for analyst and patient—is a fact in the light of which the confrontation around third party payments seems disproportionate. Instead, the author urges that this problem be approached on the technical level. Only in this way can it be addressed realistically and with a hope for solutions. Without attempting to ignore the difficulties and contradictions arising from insurance financing, the author concludes that psychoanalysis can dispense with third party financing only at the price of social isolation and therapeutic stagnation, citing the situation of psychoanalysis in the United States as an example.

Freud adopted the themes and concepts of romantic literature, which had been eliminated by the scientistic experimental psychology of his time, and made them scientific. Several points demonstrated the affinity between literature and psychoanalysis: the interpretation of dreams as model for the interpretation of literature, the dream work as analogue to the work of the writer's imagination, analogies between therapeutic and poetic economics, and the fact that Freud analyzed literary characters on the same level as real persons.

Psyche. XXXV, 1981

Siegfried Bernfeld: Historian of Psychoanalysis and Biographer of Freud. Ilse Grubrich-Simitis. Pp. 397-434.

Freud's Earliest Theories and the Helmholtz School. Siegfried Bernfeld. Pp. 435-455.

Honoring the one hundred twenty-fifth anniversary of Freud's birth, the May issue of Psyche contains preprints from two important works about to be published by Suhrkamp and S. Fischer: Siegfried Bernfeld's collected biographical studies of Freud and a supplemental volume of about seventy psychological papers by Freud which are not included in the Gesammelte Werke. Grubrich-Simitis, who was able to inspect Bernfeld's legacy, gives a sketch of his life and discusses the development of his studies of the history of psychoanalysis and his collaboration with Ernest Jones. In his paper, "Freud's Earliest Theories and the Helmholtz School," Bernfeld describes the lines of tradition within which Freud developed his psychology of the unconscious. Brücke, Freud's teacher, belonged to the generation of materialist physiologists who rejected Schelling's philosophy of nature and yet remained its heirs. Also included in the May issue are a short prefatory note by Grubrich-Simitis, a brief introduction to Freud's writings on hypnotism and suggestion by A. Harris, and three articles by Freud as part of Psyche's "Archives of Psychoanalysis" series: the Preface to his translation of Bernheim (1888), his handbook article, "Hypnosis" (1891), and the Preface to his translation of Charcot (1892-1894).

DISCUSSION: Dr. Eleanor Galenson stressed her agreement with Dr. Blos's emphasis on the girl's preoedipal maternal attachment and on the adolescent girl's struggle over oral regressive impulses. She withheld judgment, however, on his explanation of superego differences. Regarding the observed infantile roots of female development, Dr. Galenson pointed out that the only biologic neonatal variable which has been demonstrated to persist on a sex-linked basis is the genital anatomical one. During the first year of life, while boys and girls behave differently, the reason for the differences has not been clarified. During the second year, masturbatory patterns in girls change following the discovery of sexual differences—some girls foregoing masturbation, others substituting nonmanual masturbation. Dr. Galenson did not agree that penis envy is aroused defensively to ward off aggression and regression to the early mother. Instead, she and Dr. Roiphe see penis envy as arising prior to the marked increase in hostility to the mother resulting from the realization of sexual differences followed by oral and anal regressions; only then is penis envy fused with earlier disappointments in mother.

By Karl Jaspers. Translated by Oskar Grunow and David Woloshin. Tucson: University of Arizona Press, 1977. 200 pp.

Donald Burnham

Donald Burnham

Donald L. Burnham
BETHESDA, MD.

Donald Burnham  

Strindberg, to the study of whom one half of this book is devoted, has been a subject of great interest to German-speaking psychiatrists and psychoanalysts. During his lifetime he was, to his great ire, discussed by Wilhelm Hirsch as an example of mental "degeneration," then a popular concept in psychiatry.

Alfred Adler based much of his exposition of the "inferiority complex" on Strindberg's autobiographical novel, Son of a Servant. In a sort of return to the source, Adler's concept was used as a principal motif by Torsten Eklund in his biographical study of Strindberg, which he also titled Son of a Servant.

Storch's 1922 monograph, The Primitive Archaic Forms of Inner Experiences and Thought in Schizophrenia, drew heavily upon Strindberg's description of his experiences during his so-called Inferno period. In 1924 Robert Waelder's first published paper, "The Psychoses: Their Mechanisms and Accessibility to Influence," made note of Strindberg's partial recovery as an example of restitutional processes in schizophrenia. Lou Andreas-Salomé devoted a monograph to the dissection of Strindberg's troubles with sex and women. There seems to have been an element of striking back, since Strindberg had voiced very cutting opinions about women, particularly about professional women of feminist bent. Andreas-Salomé described Strindberg as a "poet … shocker-psychologist … whose men trembled not before God like master-builders but before everyday women 'satanized'!"1 An earlier antagonist was Laura Marholm, an acquaintance of Frau Lou.

1See Binion, R.: Frau Lou. Princeton, N.J.: Princeton Univ. Press, 1968, p. 179.153

Bécache presents two cases of anorgastic patients, both of whom unconsciously equated orgasm and madness. She compares this unconscious fantasy with the behavior of certain psychotic patients who are anorgastic in heterosexual relationships and rarely achieve orgasm in homosexual liaisons, but who readily achieve orgastic pleasure in masturbation. These psychotics have a fear of losing control of their aggression and of making the other person mad or destroying him. To achieve successful orgasm, they need as secure a guarantee as possible against destructive fantasies in themselves or others. At the moment of orgasm, such individuals fear self-fragmentation. The author sees evidence of this unconscious fantasy in the myth of Orpheus and Eurydice.

Chambon emphasizes the importance of pregenital and oedipal fantasies which underlie frigidity. He presents case histories in which the multiple fantasies associated with difficulties in orgastic response are detailed. The qualities of orgasm can be explained from an economic point of view in terms of proportionality and equilibrium of cathexes and countercathexes of unconscious fantasy representations. He discusses some symbolic equivalents of orgasm and finds such activities as fishing and card playing, in which there is a crescendo and a decrescendo of struggle, as containing an unconscious equation with orgastic experience.

Cournut discusses what he calls the fantasy of the infinite female orgasm. The male, proud of provoking this response, is nonetheless like the sorcerer's apprentice, overwhelmed by what has been provoked. Cournut refers to some literary examples in which curiosity and mystery surround the female orgasm and the fantasy that it is infinite. Underlying this is often a fear of castration and of loss of control, especially of sphincter control. To understand this fantasy he sketches a metapsychological explanation of the events at orgasm.

By Hans W. Loewald, M.D. New Haven and London: Yale University Press, 1980. 434 pp.

George Allison

George Allison

George H. Allison
SEATTLE, WASH

George Allison  

This collection of Loewald's papers, edited and compiled by Loewald himself, affords an opportunity to study the development and progression of a major psychoanalytic theoretician's thought over a span of thirty years. The volume, containing twenty-four articles, is divided into two sections: "Concepts and Theory" and "Pyschoanalytic Process." Loewald acknowledges that his placement of a paper in one division rather than the other is arbitrary at times, but the division is useful nevertheless. The papers are arranged by chronology, and for most of them a brief introductory footnote is provided, giving the context in which they were written or originally presented.

The "Concepts and Theory" section begins with three papers from the early 1950's which contain the beginnings of Loewald's innovations, elaborations, and revisions of key psychoanalytic theoretical issues. They include ideas about the development of the mature ego, through progressively more highly integrated and organized stages, out of the internalization of object relationships; new emphases on castration anxiety and the negative oedipus complex; and the evolution of the sense of reality and the organization of instinctual drives out of the mother-child interactional matrix. Loewald from early on showed an interest in ego defects and called for a new emphasis on the ego's integrative and organizing functions as opposed to its defensive functions. These papers, as well as his more familiar, later ones, are profound and sweeping in their scope. They occasionally include a philosophical and cultural perspective that adds richness and complexity, but they are clinically relevant and firmly based on the author's psychoanalytic experience in treating patients. The revisions and elaborations he presents are thoughtfully and creatively applied to many clinical and theoretical issues.

Richard Green  

After reading this book's Foreword by Otto Kernberg, I expected a treatise which would tell me a great deal about anorexia nervosa and give me the benefit of the experience of a psychiatrist who has been involved with the subject for over twenty-five years. In the author's Preface, I read that "this book is written in the hope of bringing together a vast amount of literature for clinicians interested in treating the anorexic" (p. xv). However, in a book of three hundred seventy-nine pages of text only twenty-two are devoted to treatment. This is one of several disappointments in an otherwise useful book.

The bulk of the book is divided into two parts. Chapter Two is a two-hundred-page novella about a mid-adolescent anorexic girl who eventually succumbs to the ravages of self-starvation. Sours cites Freud's clinical case histories, which are celebrated for their language and their sensitivity.

The silence that all too frequently greets original and genuine advancements of psychoanalytic thought is as mystifying as the din accompanying hollow, pars pro toto pseudoinnovations. No less puzzling is the seeming lack of connection between a supposedly innovative theory's popularity among psychoanalysts and its allegiance to fundamental Freudian principles and discoveries. To take an obvious example, Kohut's self psychology, however one adjudges its originality, value, and correctness, has received enormous attention and publicity in spite of—or because of—its counter-Freudian treatment of the unconscious, repression, psychosexual development, and the oedipal transformation of the self. At the same time, many original clinical contributions that elaborate, expand, deepen, and at times correct classical theories, without uprooting them wholesale, are temporarily consigned to oblivion.

It is within this framework that the work of George Devereux must be situated, with the hopeful addendum that reports of its consignment to oblivion may be premature. Over the past fortyfive years Devereux's output in the fields of psychoanalysis, anthropology, and classical literature and civilization has been prolific, provocative, and startlingly original. In his mastery of these three separate disciplines and in his original, interdisciplinary contributions to them, Devereux is in a class by himself.

Classification of Elective Mutism. Torey L. Hayden. Pp. 118-133.

In this study of sixty-eight children displaying elective mutism, four types of mutism are distinguished: (a) symbiotic mutism, characterized by a symbiotic relationship with a caretaker and a submissive but manipulative relationship with others; (b) speech phobic mutism, characterized by fear of hearing one's own voice and use of ritualistic behaviors; (c) reactive mutism, characterized by withdrawal and depression which apparently resulted from trauma; and (d) passive-aggressive mutism, characterized by hostile use of silence as a weapon. The prevalence of physical and sexual child abuse in all four groups was high. The classification of elective mutism into subgroups is clinically relevant for a better understanding of the etiology and for devising appropriate intervention.

Long-Term Outcome of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder in Childhood. Charles E. Hollingsworth, et al. Pp. 134-144.

A review of the records of one psychiatric clinic over a sixteen-year period revealed seventeen patients who met the criteria for a diagnosis of severe obsessive-compulsive neurosis. Retrospective review of these cases revealed that eighty-two per cent of the children's parents themselves suffered from severe psychiatric or medical impairment, and that twenty-nine per cent of the children suffered from serious medical illnesses. All seventeen patients had been treated, most with "intensive" psychotherapy. Fifteen patients could be located for follow-up, of whom ten agreed to a structured interview. Seven of the ten still suffered from obsessive-compulsive symptoms, and all reported serious problems with social life and peer relationships. The authors hypothesize that the obsessive-compulsive symptoms of the children served as a defense against anxiety generated by their extremely stressful life situations. The children's intellectual cognitive style and the availability in some instances of obsessive-compulsive parental models may have contributed to their choice of an obsessive-compulsive defense.

March 17, 1980. PANEL DISCUSSION: THE CONCEPT OF DEVELOPMENT IN PSYCHOANALYSIS. Melvin A. Scharfman, M.D., Moderator; Samuel Abrams, M.D.; Alan J. Eisnitz, M.D.; Jules Glenn, M.D.

Dr. Samuel Abrams described the confusion surrounding the definition of the word "development." This is partially based on the many differing psychoanalytic theories which employ the term to describe unique events. Development defined in a conventional manner can be used in the sense of an occurrence (fate), an outcome of a sequence of related events whose causal links may be traced (such as the transference neurosis), or an enhancement (the lifting of social inhibitions or the broadening of social interactions). Psychoanalysis also includes propositions of development as a process—that is, expectable progressive sequences of growth to be seen in longitudinal observations of children and in reconstruction in adult analyses. The process meaning of the word is embedded in the phrases "development orientation" and "developmental point of view." Psychoanalytic developmental psychology is based on a view of growth as a progressive differentiation and integration of discriminating constituents. A "developmental orientation" is closer to empirical data and less abstract than the "developmental point of view." The latter is conceptually analogous to the dynamic or structural point of view. It is found as a component of the "genetic hypothesis" which contains both developmental and historical propositions. The developmental component rests on several postulates: (1) intrinsic maturational factors, (2) external stimuli, and (3) experiences. The potential is fully realized in the form of a sequence of stable hierarchically ordered phase organizations. Each new phase integrates its antecedents. Steps in growth involve transformations of earlier achievements. The result is a continuity of function and a discontinuance of the mediating structures and prior organized phases.

Phases are labeled in a variety of ways and provide yet another source of confusion. They can be described as hypothetical coordinates in accordance with Freud's original approach—that is, as clinically observable characteristics, primary achievements, crises, the inherent structural makeup of the stabilized organization, or a combination of these. Sequential organizations may co-exist, overlap, or remain sharply distinct. The highly specialized use of the term development to define a process or progressive growth based on a set of postulates is most ambiguous because it is applied in so many different ways.

February 12, 1980. THE PRE-OEDIPAL DEVELOPMENT OF THE BOY. Eleanor Galenson, M.D. and Herman Roiphe, M.D.

Sigmund Freud distinguished early infantile masturbation, which usually disappears after a short time, from the revival of the sexual instincts belonging to the genital zone some time after infancy, usually before the fourth year of life. He later stated that the two sexes develop in parallel fashion until the child's observation of the anatomical difference between the sexes gives rise to the castration complex in the boy. Loewenstein contributed to the theory of sexual development, relating observations of preoedipal genital discovery in the male infant to body image disturbances observed in the analysis of an adult male. Greenacre believed that genital stimulation may occur much earlier than the phallic phase under conditions of extreme stress to the infant. Sachs and particularly Kleeman studied genital sexuality in the second year of life.

Disordered Thinking and Communication in Children

By Mahin Hassibi and Harry Breuer, Jr. New York/London: Plenum Press, 1980. 207 pp.

Theodore Shapiro

Theodore Shapiro

Theodore Shapiro
NEW YORK

Theodore Shapiro  

This volume presents a thorough clinical review of some of the issues in clinical practice with children that concern language development and disability. It provides an adequate background for the definition of linguistic problems in childhood psychoses and varieties of dysphasia and aphasia. The stages of development of language are spelled out to allow for the reader's fullest grasp of the role of cognitive and linguistic determinants. The way in which language, looked at as an autonomous function, applies to general ego organization is also considered. There are summary chapters on diagnosis and the interpretation of psychological testing of dysphasic and psychotic children.

The chapter concerning childhood psychosis will be of special interest to the psychiatrist. The authors present a thoroughgoing historical review and perspective on the problems that have confronted child psychiatrists in recognizing and diagnosing autism and schizophrenia in childhood. The changing trends in diagnostic emphasis parallel aspects of the changing trends in diagnosis in American psychiatry as a whole. This chapter also provides the readers with help in discerning the problem with which child psychiatrists struggle in their relationship to other professionals who deal with children.

[[RunningHead]]

The Narcissistic Pursuit of Perfection

By Arnold Rothstein, M.D. New York: International Universities Press, Inc., 1980. 287 pp.

Burness Moore

Burness Moore

Burness E. Moore
ATLANTA

Burness Moore  

In this book, Rothstein seeks to lessen the great confusion that has arisen about the concept of narcissism by limiting the term "narcissism" to a "felt quality of perfection,… this conscious or unconscious, affectively laden fantasy… invested in a panoply of self-and/or object-representations in a spectrum of integrations" (p. 4). The content, he says, has affective, physical, and cognitive components. What is common to all is a superlative designation. This definition is qualified by the statement that "the pursuit of perfection may be invested, for example, in phallic activities derived primarily from oedipal issues and conflicts. However, whatever the narcissistic investment, it is associatively linked to pre-individuated fixation points of perfection that remain unconscious and in a state of primary repression" (p. 18).

This central thesis is based in part on the observation that "Freud used the term narcissism to describe a felt quality of perfection and as a prestructural concept to describe the development of psychic structure in response to ubiquitous narcissistic injuries" (p. 5). In the quoted reference Freud did say that narcissism is displaced onto a new ideal ego in an attempt to recover the lost perfection of childhood. Rothstein's use of Freud's statement to justify a concept of undifferentiated narcissism throughout life is subject to serious question, however.

Rothstein defines narcissism as the pursuit of perfection, and he views the means for attaining it in a way that conforms to Stolorow's definition of narcissism as mental activity functioning to "maintain the structural cohesiveness, temporal stability and positive affective colouring of the self-representation."1

1Stolorow, R. D. (1975). Toward a functional definition of narcissism. Int. J. Psychoanal., 56:179.439

James McLaughlin

James McLaughlin

James T. McLaughlin
PITTSBURGH

James McLaughlin  

In 1976, Leo Stone and Robert Langs sat down together for the first of six audiotaped meetings which Stone understood were to be "quite casual, informal conversations" (p. ix) about their perceptions of the psychoanalytic situation and its experiences. That these meetings turned out to be neither casual nor conversational, but instead had a formidable agenda and a definite intent, he quickly discovered.

Langs was "primed for debate" (p. ix). He showed anticipatory uneasiness over exposing himself to criticism and discomfort about engaging in dispute with a bold and more experienced colleague (p. vii), but he also evinced satisfaction that the basic structure of his theories was well established (p. viii).

What is hinted at in these prefatory remarks receives fuller exposition in the book than one would wish to have. It is reiterated throughout more than three hundred pages of dialogue in a carelessly edited book that is as tedious as it is stimulating and as repetitious and circling as it is informative and fresh.

[[RunningHead]]

Forms of Brief Therapy

Edited by Simon H. Budman. New York and London: The Guilford Press, 1981. 482 pp.

Maxwell Soll

Maxwell Soll

Maxwell H. Soll
DALLAS

Maxwell Soll  

This volume, which grew out of the Harvard Community Health Plan Conference on brief therapy in 1979, is composed of a collection of papers representing the work of various clinicians and researchers in the field of the brief therapies. I deliberately use the plural because, rather than focusing on any one form of brief therapy, the book covers a multitude of approaches. These range from analytically oriented individual therapy (in itself including various and contrasting theoretical and technical approaches) to behavioral, marital, and group therapies. The general tenor of the book is one of rather impressive optimism that the short-term therapies either now or in the near future will meet the pressing needs of the large majority of psychiatric patients, both in terms of clinical improvement—or even cure—and cost effectiveness.

Herbert Pardes, Director of NIMH and a psychoanalyst, and Harold Pincus offer an overview of the way in which brief therapy relates to national mental health issues. They stress the nation's great unmet need for mental health services, the difficulties certain segments of the population have experienced in utilizing available services, the increasing concerns about burgeoning costs to government and other third-party payers, and the historical aspects of the growth of community mental health centers and health maintenance organizations as providers of psychiatric care. They believe that within a context of appropriate technological advance, particularly with emphasis on specificity and differentiation of intervention modalities and accurate assessment of treatment results, brief therapy promises to promote wider and better care for a wide variety of psychiatric patients. Indeed, a recurring theme expressed by many of the authors in this book is the need for proper attention to the patient-therapist fit and for specificity of treatment techniques tailored to the particular problems with which patients present themselves.

The historical development culminating in the American and French Revolutions in the second half of the eighteenth century finally succeeded, in most Western countries, in destroying feudal bondage and in granting civil rights to individuals. Melvin Stanger

Melvin Stanger

Melvin Stanger  

This is the kind of necessary and useful paper that should be read by all who care about the successful operation of the educational programs within our psychoanalytic institutes and who are concerned about the further development and training of the psychoanalytic faculty. The authors first describe the operations of the selection committee at the Denver Psychoanalytic Institute, with specific attention to the evolution of the committee's decision-making process and to its own program of education and training for new committee members. In the second section of the paper, the authors discuss in some detail the qualities they believe necessary in candidates for the committee. Finally, the authors give three examples of the selection process. In each of these the clinical data of the interviews is presented, the analytic thinking of the selector as he listened and processed the material is discussed, and the selection committee's discussion and recommendation is described.

475

The Annual of Psychoanalysis. VII, 1978

The Sustaining Object Relationship. Howard Levine. With discussion by Marian Tolpin and a rejoinder from Howard Levine. Pp. 203-231.

Melvin Stanger

Melvin Stanger

Melvin Stanger  

Levine describes, with detailed clinical examples, a group of patients who do not have a firm and cohesive sense of self and have not obtained libidinal object constancy. The continued durability of the self and the object is therefore contingent upon a continued relationship with a real or fantasied object, which Levine calls the sustaining object relationship. Since this object is so important to patients, they must attempt to control it because the loss of the relationship can be life-threatening. But at the same time, the fear of engulfment, the wish to merge, and the fear of retaliation that such a relationship may produce can be equally threatening. The author feels that a "narcissistic alliance" is essential for treatment of these patients, one in which the analyst can assume the role of the sustaining object until gradual stability of the patient's self and object world can be achieved independently of the analyst's function. At this point the analyst can return to his function of analyzing in the usual way those intrapsychic conflicts that produce neurotic symptoms and inhibitions. In a discussion of this paper, Tolpin differentiates patients who have disorders of self-cohesion secondary to regressions from those who have true disorders of the self. In the former group, it is really preoedipal pathology that serves as a defense against phallic-oedipal conflicts, and those patients should be analyzed in the classical way. However, in the other group, with primary pathology of the self, the correct treatment requires the development of the self-object transference and its gradual interpretation through transmuting internalizations. In his well-reasoned rejoinder, the author points out that one cannot so sharply separate preoedipal regressions from primary pathology of the self. There are patients with a mixed picture of predominantly oedipal-preoedipal problems together with primary pathology of the self. Levine also properly questions the idea that patients with primary self-cohesion who have been treated through analysis in the manner of Kohut are now completely analyzed. What has happened to their oedipal conflicts?

In this stimulating paper, the author describes some of his analytic work with two gifted male patients, which has led him to arrive at some general conclusions concerning the psychology of genius. The author also briefly contrasts these two patients' development with that of Sigmund Freud. He concludes by giving us a psychobiographical cameo of Friedrich Nietzsche's life, focusing particularly on the threats to their self-esteem that parents experience when their children appear to be different or odd.

Holland analyzes the dream of Hermia in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream on a number of different levels and from different points of view, one of which includes the author's personal associations and feelings as they relate to his own life and times, as he hears the dream. This method, with which the author wishes us to become familiar as a new kind of psychoanalytic method with literature, is called "transactive criticism," and it does succeed in further enriching the meaning of the particular dream for us by adding to it both a contemporary and a personal dimension.

479

The author uses Oscar Wilde's novel to show the discrepancy experienced between one's self-representation as offered by another and as arising primarily from within. He shows how the main character first accepts as his own the

479

distorted representations of him given by others and then attempts to rid himself of the effects of these distorted perceptions. I feel that this paper is of particular interest in that it furthers understanding of certain kinds of narcissistic and homosexual relationships (in fact Wilde must have been writing about himself), and it also touches on some psychodynamic elements which are of significance in "brainwashing."

480

Ronald Krasner

Ronald Krasner

Ronald Krasner  

In this 1962 paper, Max Deutscher (1916-1979), to whom this entire issue is dedicated, attempts to outline the development of a man's sense of fatherhood during the course of his wife's pregnancy. It is complementary to the woman's regressive identifications with her mother in a search for her motherliness. It "is the man's search for the personifications in his history for his own fatherliness." Two cases are presented, and Deutscher concludes by stating that in the man a particular shift must occur whereby the infantile and narcissistic elements are transformed into a healthy paternal love after the birth of the child.

481

In treating patients whose psychopathology is the consequence of an early developmental arrest, the analyst must be able to distinguish between archaic pre-stages of transference and manifestations of classical transference neurosis. In such cases, the correct assessment of the quality of the therapeutic relationship enables the analyst to adopt a therapeutic stance which gradually promotes the structuralization of precarious self- and object representations. A specific type of transference-countertransference disjunction may preclude this requisite therapeutic stance. While Kohut has attributed such countertransferences to the analyst's own narcissistic disturbance, the authors suggest they are more typically a technical error of interpreting remnants of developmental arrests as if they were expressions of resistances defending against intrapsychic conflicts. Negative therapeutic reactions, they believe, may stem from failure to recognize the arrested developmental aspects of the patient's psychopathology, so that vital developmental requirements revived in relation to the analyst once again meet with traumatically unempathic responses. Successful treatment would thus depend in large part on the analyst's ability to achieve a correct empathic grasp of the patient's subjective experience in the analytic relationship.

Ein Leben Für Die Psychoanalyse. Anmerkungen Zu Meiner Zeit. (A Life for Psychoanalysis. Remarks on my Times.)

By Alexander Mitscherlich. Frankfurt am Main: Suhrkamp Verlag, 1980. 323 pp.

Yela Lowenfeld

Yela Lowenfeld

Yela Lowenfeld
NEW YORK

Yela Lowenfeld  

One may call this book an intellectual autobiography or, even better, a psychological one. The author looks back upon his life's development with the eyes of a psychoanalyst. He concentrates upon those influences and factors which seem to him to have had the strongest impact upon him. Devoting a good deal of space to recollections of his childhood, he describes the way in which his parents, the social climate, and his environment seem to have formed his character. Mitscherlich was born and raised in a provincial town in Bavaria as the only child of a well-to-do factory owner. His childhood was lonely and joyless. His father, reactionary and unbending, had little understanding for his shy and musing son. His mother, although warm-hearted, was not strong enough to provide an emotionally secure surrounding for him. His loneliness became even more painful in grammar school where his classmates were the children of the factory workers. They treated him, the director's son, with aggressive contempt, as he was better dressed than they were and was refined and shy. He felt awkward, isolated, and guilty. He dates his never diminishing interest in social problems and in mass psychology to these early school years.

In his adolescence he searched for a mentor whom he could admire and love. He respected the strength of his father, but he could not love him. It was particularly difficult to find his ideal in those years of rapidly growing National Socialism. From the very beginning he abhorred the brutality and racism. His first personal experience with Nazi ideology took place at the University of Munich. He was studying history and working on his doctoral thesis under a Jewish professor. After that professor's death in 1932 his successor refused to continue the work, declaring that studies done under a Jew were worthless.

Mitscherlich understood immediately that it would be meaningless and dishonest to study history in the climate of National Socialism.

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman  

Kernberg, in his inimitably clear, condensed, highly organized style, again details his approach to the psychoanalytically oriented treatment of borderline patients. Above all, he repeatedly cautions that a combination of expressive and supportive therapy is contraindicated, strongly favoring a firmly held position of technical neutrality by the therapist throughout the long, arduous course of treatment. This "nonsupportive" technique is, in the long run, the only one truly supportive of full, reconstructive personality development. The author emphasizes that "technical neutrality" does not imply lack of empathy. Focusing specifically on the diagnosis of borderline conditions in adolescents as opposed to schizophrenia or normal turmoil, Kernberg reiterates his diagnostic criteria of "identity diffusion," predominance of primitive defensive operations, especially splitting, and maintenance of reality testing. Careful diagnosis is essential for selection of proper treatment. Kernberg feels that if family therapy is indicated in the treatment of borderline adolescents, it should be done by someone other than the adolescent's own therapist. He feels that the developmental tasks of adolescence in the borderline can best be accomplished through the same psychotherapeutic technique appropriate to the therapy of the older borderline. Finally, he considers the problem of acting out in the therapy of the borderline adolescent, describes various forms it takes, and recommends that a team approach be used if external structure is required, leaving the therapist free to work within the technical analytic framework.

ABSTRACT

What seems at first to be a humanistic trend in recent psychoanalytic thinking may actually be the culmination of a holistic movement that began soon after Freud. As theory, it carries with it many built-in difficulties and requires implicit support from the partializing parent theory. In the shadow of that older theory, however, it makes a number of important contributions, including attention to meaning as made, not just discovered, and the importance of the analyst's attitudes in treatment.

This paper critically evaluates fundamental concepts of object relations theory with reference to both cognitive theory and developmental theory. For example, Melanie Klein's view that objects are a permanent unchanging substratum of personality acquired in infancy is challenged as placing too much emphasis on an inner world and too little on the external world and its ongoing influence. While object relations theory makes a noteworthy contribution to a psychoanalytic view of personality, in the opinion of the author it overlooks important observations from cognitive and developmental psychology.

On Sexuality: Psychoanalytic Observations

Edited by Toksoz B. Karasu, M.D. and Charles W. Socarides, M.D. New York: International Universities Press, Inc., 1979. 412 pp.

Phyllis Tyson

Phyllis Tyson

Phyllis Tyson
LA JOLLA, CALIF.

Phyllis Tyson  

Karasu and Socarides have chosen articles that blend psychoanalytic insights with applied psychoanalytic, sociopsychological, historical, anthropological, educational, and philosophical considerations. The articles vary widely in their quality and in their relevance to psychoanalysis. Three broad aspects of sexuality are addressed: development, deviance, and related social issues. One curious note is that in a book purporting to deal with the psychoanalytic theory of sexuality the phallic phase is mentioned only in passing.

The well-known work of Eleanor Galenson and Herman Roiphe begins the section on development. They have demonstrated that the child's discovery of anatomical differences takes place earlier than Freud hypothesized and that boys and girls react to it differently. Although they confirm Freud's emphasis on the girl's vulnerability to penis envy and castration fantasies, they question his conclusion that this is the initiator of oedipal phase development. Galenson and Roiphe emphasize that the girl's reactions are determined largely by earlier experiences and by the quality of her relationships with her parents.

We must recognize that there is not full agreement with all of Galenson and Roiphe's theoretical conclusions. They postulate, for example, that the development of symbolic functioning in girls appears to be influenced by their reactions to the discovery of the difference between the sexes and that a severe castration reaction predisposes a girl to a negative oedipal libidinal organization. A considerable number of variables, including aspects of object relations, genetic constitution, and cognitive functioning, however, must also be considered to understand the evolution of symbolic functioning and of the girl's oedipal development.

From the sexual concerns of two year olds we advance to an account of the current sexual attitudes of adolescents. Aaron H. Esman, in a sociological, anthropological, and cultural study of adolescence, offers the opinion that despite the fears of the older generation, the greatest changes in adolescents created by the so-called "sexual revolution" is not an increase of promiscuity or perversion, but a reduction in sexual inhibitions and guilt.

Highland Hospital

Asheville, N.C. 28802

Robert Frick  

ABSTRACT

Recent research has demonstrated important integrating and organizing functions of the cerebellum and vestibular nuclei considerably beyond their conventionally accepted roles in somatic motor coordination. There are major parallels between the newer, expanded concepts of vestibulocerebellar function and the current psychoanalytic understanding of ego functions. This article reviews the various usages of the term "ego" and especially focuses on the principles of ego psychology as developed by Heinz Hartmann. It then reviews the extensive research on nonmotor vestibulocerebellar system (VCS) functions. Finally, it examines significant parallels between ego functions and VCS functions within motor, sensory, vegetative, emotional, and intellectual spheres.

Meetings of the Psychoanalytic Association of New York

October 20, 1980. THE NEW PSYCHOSOMATIC MEDICINE. Lawrence Deutsch, M.D.

Dr. Deutsch addressed the important challenges for our profession raised by "the new psychosomatic medicine." He observed that the use of the term "psychosomatic," once restricted to the so-called "holy seven" illnesses described by Alexander, has now been broadened to include virtually all illness. Accordingly, psychoanalysts, once the guiding lights of the psychosomatic movement, are being replaced by the social epidemiologists and the neuroendocrinologists. Dr. Deutsch decried this trend, noting that while there is much to learn from the other disciplines which comprise holistic medicine, analysts are in a unique position to provide the understanding necessary if there is to be synthesis of the psychological, sociological, and physiological aspects of disease. Analysts must resume their role in the treatment of the classical psychosomatic disorders. Dr. Deutsch proposed that the term "psychosomatic" be retained for the classical diseases so described and that a new term, such as "biopsychosocial," be used when talking about the new holistic medicine.

Dr. Deutsch discussed social epidemiology in some detail. The literature is filled with large population studies in which morbidity and mortality from a variety of diseases are positively correlated with antecedent stress, such as retirement, natural catastrophe, and bereavement. Work on the correlation between the "type A personality" and coronary heart disease has been extensive. But the work of the social epidemiologists is, by definition, on "populations at risk." The understanding of how these diverse stresses lead to physical illness can best be achieved by examination of the affective, symbolic, and unconscious impact of the "stressful event" on a given individual, a kind of understanding that psychoanalysts are in a position to provide. Analytic interviews and psychological testing might provide data concerning the relationship between morbidity and antecedent behavior. "Dynamic understanding of the variety of conflicts and structural defects that can lead to morbidity would allow for a more meaningful set of findings and better utilization of these." Dr. Deutsch emphasized the potential complementarity of the approaches of social epidemiologists and psychoanalysts. Large population studies lead to attempts at environmental manipulation. The insights of analysis would be invaluable in helping us to understand the meaning of the stress on a given individual or type of individual and would allow us "to fine-tune the nature of our interventions.

Martin Silverman M.D.

Martin Silverman

Martin A. Silverman, M.D.
551 Ridgewood Rd.
Maplewood, N.J. 07040

Martin Silverman  

ABSTRACT

A nine-year-old boy in analysis for behavior and learning problems developed an intense transference reaction marked by increasing excitement and competitive anxiety. These were traceable to scopophilic interests, primal scene excitement, and oedipal rivalries. When his father underwent surgery close to the genitals, the child's conflicts surfaced with such intensity that he no longer was able to effectively master them through play and verbal expression alone. He solved his dilemma by making symbolic use of the telephone as a means of representing his masturbatory fantasies and the guilts and fears associated with them. Not only could his symbolic use of the telephone be observed as it came into being, but its utilization for the purposes of defense, mastery, conflict resolution, and the facilitation of developmental progression could be explored and understood.

[[RunningHead]]

An Unusual Infantile Theory of the Origin of the Female Sex

Joseph Slap M.D.

Joseph Slap

Joseph W. Slap, M.D.
1601 Walnut St.
Philadelphia, Pa. 19102

Joseph Slap  

Abraham (1923) reported a patient's dream which revealed her theory of how she came to be born a female: in the dream the patient was lying on the ground under water when a man in a boat plunged a pole into her three times, boring holes in the region of her mouth, her breast, and her abdomen. Abraham understood the latent content of this dream as a fantasy in which the father's penis damaged the patient in utero thus determining her gender.

Such fantasies are not uncommon in my experience. Recently, however, I came across an unusual variation on this fantasy. A patient, who suffered from feelings of castration and who evidenced a wish to bite off her father's penis, with talionic fantasies of having her teeth fall out, had been struggling to recall details of a primal scene experience which occurred when she was a little past her fourth birthday. Her mother at that time was in the ninth month of pregnancy with the patient's sister, Karen, her only sibling. Dreams, associations, and transference phenomena—along with her dim memory of the event—suggested that her mother refused to have intercourse with the father out of a fear of harming the baby and that the patient's parents had performed "sixty-nine" instead.

During this period of analysis I hung a new graphic in the office, a Motherwell aquatint which consisted of an amorphous black shape superimposed on a background of red. The patient took an instant dislike to this print and described it as a "hairy monster." During a session a few weeks after it was hung, she said that she had been obsessed with it during the night; it had seemed to pursue her.

Color in the Dreams of the Color-Blind

Richard Yazmajian M.D.

Richard Yazmajian

Richard V. Yazmajian, M.D.
85 Creston Ave.
Tenafly, N.J. 07670

Richard Yazmajian  

ABSTRACT

This paper attempts to illustrate how three color-blind patients utilized color in their dreams in such a manner as to actively deny their visual defect. These patients had displaced to the eyes some critical conflicts about other body parts. The use of color to deny color blindness thus further served to deny other physical defects, both real and imaginary. In addition, this defense helped to fend off intense affects related to these defects as well as associated castration anxieties.

Clinical Studies in Infant Mental Health. The First Year of Life

Edited by Selma Fraiberg,1 with the collaboration of Louis Fraiberg. New York: Basic Books, Inc., 1980. 279 pp.

Scott Dowling

Scott Dowling

Scott Dowling
CLEVELAND

Scott Dowling  

Ever since The Magic Years charmed its way into our parental and professional hearts, each new book or article by Selma Fraiberg and her collaborators has been a special occasion. We have come to expect solid scholarship, ingenious investigative techniques, precise theoretical reasoning, and warm compassion, all presented in a spirited and lucid literary style.

Clinical Studies in Infant Mental Health continues this tradition. The studies reported here began in 1972 in the Child Development Project in Ann Arbor. They grew out of Professor Fraiberg's work with blind infants. The Infant Mental Health Program proposed to provide assessment and treatment services for "disadvantaged infants and their parents." The carefully documented development of these services would comprise the research component of the program. There would be no fees. For those who have worked with socially and economically disadvantaged, severely disturbed infant-mother pairs, the boldness implicit in such an invitation is impressive. This was not to be a survey or consultation service or a well-protected research study. Furthermore, there were no models for program development or for assessment and treatment methods, with the one significant exception of their own program for blind infants. With her small band of co-workers, Professor Fraiberg chose to leap straight into the vortex of the problem, inviting no-fee referrals from all agencies and hospitals of Washtenaw County. The expectable deluge of impossible cases arrived.

1Selma Fraiberg died in December 1981. She was one of America's most accomplished and productive child analysts. Her theoretical and clinical contributions to child analysis and to applied analysis, including seminal observations on blind infants and deprived infants, have been unique. This review was written prior to her death.430

Boons suggests that the "propaganda" about orgasm is a reversal of the Victorian injunction against women enjoying sex, which now returns as an imperative to enjoy sex. She sees this as a continued form of oppression and as a masculine attempt to dominate women now in an objective and research-oriented language. Boons discusses the Lacanian and structuralist analysis of orgasm, which assigns to woman's orgasm the character of being infinite. She sees this as still another example of masculine narcissism which equates women with inaccessibility and sorcery.

Revue Française De Psychanalyse. XLI, 1977

Reich's Theory of Orgasm and the Freudian Theory of Infantile Sexuality. Janine Chasseguet-Smirgel. Pp. 639-652.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

Reich attempted to found a theory of psychopathology and of psychosomatic illness around orgasm. Chasseguet-Smirgel's thesis is that Reich's work continues to contribute to the effacement of Freud's discovery of infantile sexuality. Jean Gillibert has suggested that the emphasis on sexuality today constitutes a negation and a repression of infantile sexuality. Chasseguet-Smirgel agress and argues that Reich was one of the first who attempted to eradicate Freud's fundamental discovery. Reich appears to have fought for sexual liberty and the recognition of sexuality in children, but Chasseguet-Smirgel finds that the result of his work is quite different. Reich's reduction of sexuality to genitality negates infantile sexuality and thus the whole Freudian broadening of the concept of sexuality. Reich's viewpoint also minimizes considerations of psychic structure. The superego is seen as a result of external constraint, completely detached from its biological and infantile origins. Reich even explains infantile dependency as the result of parental authority and suggests that oedipal conflicts would disappear if oppressive external constraints were absent. Chasseguet-Smirgel reviews some of the possible unconscious meanings which orgasm may have had for Reich, suggesting that Reich in effect offered us, instead of a real theory of the orgasm, a catalog of orgasm's unconscious meanings.

162

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

Flournoy claims that there are three levels of satisfaction involved in orgasm: narcissistic, pregenital, and oedipal. These three levels are also involved in the report of orgasm in the analytic situation. Flournoy believes that an impasse results, preventing the possibility of speaking successfully about orgasm in analysis. The analysis of a successful orgasm would be seen as a betrayal of the coupling in which the orgasm occurred, while the orgasm itself is seen as the betrayal of the analyst in the love for another. Just as orgasm excludes the analyst, the sharing of the report of the orgasm excludes the partner. Hence it is exceptional that a successful orgasm is reported in analysis. It is usually passed over with a comment, "It was good." Flournoy considers a case history in which a patient seemed to separate his orgasm from the actual coital ejaculation. This "after the fact" orgasm may possibly have derived from his wish to save the orgasm for the analyst.

163
