Gender Identity Conflicts in Male Transsexualism. Milton Eber. Pp. 31-38.

Sheila Gray

Sheila Gray

Sheila Gray  

A twenty-five-year-old person who had apparently met the diagnostic criteria for "true" transsexualism in his adolescence came for treatment to have the sexual

164

reversal surgery itself reversed. While the patient had made a fairly good adjustment as a female, she was unable to overcome the knowledge that she was in fact a man. Psychological evaluation revealed a primitive level of ego development with marked impulsivity and severely unstable identifications, but there was no evidence of psychosis. The patient remained in treatment for only six sessions and resumed life as a female, later requesting transformation surgery once again. Using Kubie's concept of a drive to become both sexes, the author demonstrates that in this case and in a similar one described by Stoller and Newman the gender dysphoria is not a specific complaint to be cured by specific surgery, but the manifestation of a developmental failure of separation-individuation. The solution to such problems, the author implies, is intrapsychic, not surgical.

165

[[RunningHead]]

The Therapeutic Environment

By Robert Langs, M.D. New York: Jason Aronson, 1979. 574 pp.

Stephen Firestein

Stephen Firestein

Stephen K. Firestein
NEW YORK

Stephen Firestein  

In his preface Robert Langs defines the therapeutic environment as "the ground rules, framework, hold, and setting of the psychotherapeutic and analytic situations" (p. ix). He quickly stakes out his essential thesis that "the frame itself is undoubtedly the single most fundamental component of the analytic and therapeutic interactions," and claims that patients will respond to alterations in the therapeutic environment with strong reactions that are very predictable. He states further that his experience has been that presentation of this demonstrable sequence to therapists and analysts tends to elicit highly emotional reactions, which in part seem to him to reflect countertransference phenomena.

It is this contradiction between patients' responses and therapists' reactions to alterations in the framework that Langs is addressing in the body of this lengthy volume.

Langs's approach involves application of previously described methods of listening to the patient's associations and an attempt to validate hypotheses generated by those verbalizations. These methods focus upon the manner in which the therapist manages and regulates the interaction with the patient. The meaning for the patient of the various elements in the therapeutic environment are examined through reactions to deviations in the essential elements of that environment, including the physiotemporal features and the human aspects. The reactions are viewed in terms of conscious and unconscious derivatives communicated by the patient, especially what Langs labels "Type Two Derivatives." By this latter designation Langs intends validating inferences from the patient's manifest statements that can be related to a "specific adaptive context"—that is, to a specific item in the therapeutic environment to which the patient is responding. Langs states that influences disturbing the secure, silent framework for the treatment are common. He places an emphasis upon therapeutic work focused upon such disturbances which he feels become frequently critical for the effectiveness of the treatment. He includes more than correct interpretations in his definition of this therapeutic work.

The Role of the Talionic Impulse in the Development of Morality. James F. Masterson. Pp. 482-492.

Sheila Gray

Sheila Gray

Sheila Gray  

The origin of the talionic impulse may be seen in the real or fantasied attempt to undo an early childhood trauma by actively inflicting the experience on the original perpetrator. These impulses seem initially to demand immediate release; but as the individual matures, they are internalized and mastered, becoming adult superego functions, a personal morality. In the borderline patient, there is a failure to master the talionic impulse. Instead, the patient continually repeats the trauma. Often, because of identification with the aggressor, it is directed against the self. Such patients use psychotherapy not as a way of getting better, but of "getting back." Sometimes they channel these impulses into militant efforts on behalf of social causes. For therapy to be successful, the patient must master both the talionic impulse and castration anxiety. The author suggests that this mastery forms essential roots of adult morality.

166

[[RunningHead]]

The Psychoanalytic Study of the Child. XXXIV, 1979

Children of Chowchilla. A Study of psychic Trauma. Lenore C. Terr. Pp. 547-623.

H. Blank

H. Blank

H. Blank  

On July 15, 1976, in Chowchilla, a small rural community in the San Joaquin Valley of California, three armed masked men kidnapped twenty-six children and the driver of their school bus. They were transferred into two vans and driven around in total darkness for eleven hours. At about 3:30 A.M., they were transferred one by one into a "hole," a buried truck-trailer, where they were reunited in a poorly lit large space. Food consisted of stale breakfast cereal, potato chips, peanut butter, and water. Two wheel-wells, one for boys, one for girls, were the "bathrooms." The children remained in the "hole" for sixteen hours, until the driver and several of the older boys dug an escape hatch out of the roof. The police were called and the entire group taken to a nearby prison for questioning and sporadic sleep. The children were picked up by their families the next morning; the total period of separation was about forty-three hours. The victims received no psychiatric help for five months. Three of the children left the community. The author worked with the remaining twenty-three children and their parents for eight months. There were seventeen girls and six boys ranging in age from five to fourteen years. There were seven sibling and two cousin groups. The psychiatric findings, including the immediate and long-term effects of the kidnapping on the children, the parents, and the community, are presented in detail. Some of the findings were surprising and challenging to accepted theory. For example, every one of the twenty-three children was affected by the traumatic event. All developed a variety of persistent fears and unsuccessfully attempted to cope with them. Anxiety was manifested in play, behavioral re-enactments, and repetitive dreams. Among the many anxiety dreams related to the kidnapping, five children (five to nine years old) had terrifying dreams of their own death. The age of the traumatized child did not seem to be a determinant of the severity of the post-traumatic symptoms. There was an amazing similarity of response across the entire age range.

The Paranoid Process

By W. W. Meissner, S.J., M.D. New York: Jason Aronson, Inc., 1978. 872 pp.

Arnold Richards

Arnold Richards

Arnold Richards
NEW YORK

Arnold Richards  

Few contributors to the psychoanalytic literature today would consider tackling a topic of the breadth and scope of Meissner's Paranoid Process. He has written a massive, ambitious work that is divided into three main sections. The first, titled "The Structure and Function of Paranoid Ideation," considers the psychopathology of paranoia, paranoid mechanisms, and paranoid style. It is concerned with the variety of theoretical perspectives that have been brought to bear on paranoid psychopathology, beginning with Freud's classic exposition of Schreber.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Revue Française De Psychanalyse. XLII, 1978

Mourning and the Appearance of Epileptic Seizures in Children. Bernard Soulas. Pp. 389-410.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

An interesting clinical fact is that many epileptic children experience their first seizure following a loss. Soulas investigates this correlation in order to understand psychological factors involved in epilepsy, especially the relationship between epilepsy and the death instinct. He reviews case material from two groups. The first consists of children whose first seizure came after the death of an individual who was an important object. In this group he finds a relationship between hysteria and epilepsy. He emphasizes also the importance of the mother's attitude toward her pregnancy with that child. Soulas develops two hypotheses on the meaning of death to children: one is that the fantasy of nonexistence refers to the child's ideas about what he was and where he was before he was born. This hypothesis, Soulas reminds us, is similar to Ferenczi's notion of epilepsy as a regression to an embryonic state. His second hypothesis on childhood representations of death concerns the importance of sadistic and violent destructive fantasies. Soulas's second group of cases involves children whose parents have experienced the loss of a child. The traumatic factor in these cases is the manner in which the parents react to the loss. Such parents have had difficulty in carrying out the work of mourning. The child may perhaps identify with the mother in this mourning and achieve a violent elaboration of pathological mourning in the form of epileptic seizure. No doubt the youngster has also experienced separation from the mother as traumatic. The initial epileptic seizure is often preceded by a traumatic physical incident. The initiative function of this incident probably comes about by affording the child an experience of a mechanical aggression, indicating to its ego a masochistic pathway for the expression of aggression. Soulas reviews some of the implications of his findings and makes suggestions for further research on the epileptic child, especially on the neonatal experience and the nonobjectal stages of early development.

[[RunningHead]]

Revue Française De Psychanalyse. XLII, 1978

The Fetishistic Object Relationship. Evelyne Kestemberg. Pp. 195-214.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

In this rich and insightful article, Kestemberg discusses a type of object relationship which she terms fetishistic. She develops the concept of fetish

667

familiar to us from Freud into a broader concept which serves not only as a mechanism of denial of castration, but also to preserve narcissistic integrity by projection onto a thing. In this larger concept of the fetish, the ego projects onto an object other than the self the qualities of lasting immutability, magical powers, etc., which are habitually included in the unconscious fantasies of the subject in his relationship to his own internal objects. Thus the fetishistic object relationship is one manifestation of the tendency of the human psychic apparatus toward idealization. The range of such fetishistic phenomena is great, and, indeed, probably no one is exempt from some sort of fetishistic attachment to objects which serve as guarantors of narcissistic integrity. Kestemberg's article contains many stimulating insights into the similarities and differences between her concept and Winnicott's notion of the transitional object. She considers also Melanie Klein's concept of projective identification, but places emphasis on the immutability and deanimation characteristic of the fetishistic object. A case history illustrative of this phenomenon is presented. The analyst found it necessary technically to provide "holding" in Winnicott's sense until a different and stronger organization was achieved by the patient. In a metapsychological discussion of this view of the fetish, the author distinguishes her concept of the self from those of Winnicott and Kohut. The self is, for her, the first organized configuration of the psychic apparatus which develops from the mother-child unit and is the successor to this unity. Thus the self for Kestemberg prefigures and is the source of the ego/self distinction of these other writers. The self represents the narcissistic continuity of the subject in an autoerotic fashion, in the absence of the primary object. The fetishistic object relationship is a product of this self and contributes to the organization of the ego ideal. Kestemberg's is an important study which attempts to delineate the diverse modalities of narcissistic investment and thus enriches the discussion of the concept of primary narcissism. Further, important technical considerations derive from the exploration of this concept, especially the recognition of the need for the respect for and utilization of the fetishistic relationship until the patient is able to have access to an authentic transference relationship.

668

[[RunningHead]]

The Emerging Goddess. The Creative Process in Art, Science, and Other Fields

By Albert Rothenberg, M.D. Chicago and London: University of Chicago Press, 1979. 440 pp.

Stuart Feder

Stuart Feder

Stuart Feder
NEW YORK

Stuart Feder  

In the central metaphor of The Emerging Goddess, the birth of the Goddess of Wisdom is compared to the processes which underlie all human creative endeavor. The finest products of this enterprise, be they in the physical or mental sciences, philosophy and the humanities, or the arts, are endowed with an integrated wholeness that fosters the illusion that just as Athene was born from the brow of Zeus, they have sprung forth fully integrated from the minds of their creators. Like the goddess in all her metaphorical splendor, the creation is both new and valued, the basis upon which an esthetic point of view is formed. The task which the author has set himself in this volume is to illuminate the act of creation—to describe it, to delineate the processes involved, to photograph the birth of the goddess emerging. A task so comprehensive in scope courts failure by its very magnitude. Nevertheless, although inevitable shortcomings are perceivable in the book, Rothenberg has made a unique contribution to a field whose literature is, to say the least, uneven.

Form follows function as the author, himself no mean exponent of the creative process, develops his central ideas in a highly elaborated fashion and in such a way as to engender their "emergence" over the course of the entire work. They do not lend themselves readily to pithy formulation, and the author takes pains to return to them again and again, elucidating one or another feature within different creative contexts.

Meetings of the Psychoanalytic Association of New York

November 17, 1980. SELF THEORY, CONFLICT THEORY, AND THE PROBLEM OF HYPOCHONDRIASIS. Arnold Richards, M.D.

In his presentation of the clinical case history of a patient with a narcissistic syndrome, hypochondriasis, Dr. Richards took issue with the new psychology of

491

the self and its dismissal of conflict. His patient's morbid preoccupation with self and body could not be traced simply to some evanescing self image, but had to be traced instead to those object-instinctual conflicts dealt with by classical analysis. In an earlier work Dr. Richards had questioned what he considered to be the four basic principles of Kohut's theory: 1) the concept of narcissism as evolving along a separate developmental line of object relations and drive manifestations; 2) the stress on the economic point of view and concomitantly "on contentless mental states"; 3) the reified "delineation of two specific self-object transferences"—idealizing and mirror; and 4) the emphasis on the analyst's emotional empathy to the exclusion of his powers of observation, cognition, and synthesis. According to Dr. Richards, such a constellation of views is to be faulted not because it is "revolutionary," but because the focus is too narrow to account for the data: it fails to encompass the pervasive, protean impact of unconscious conflict and the interplay of conflict and deficit as interdependent variables.

Dr. Richards's patient was referred for analysis following an unsuccessful course of psychopharmacological treatment and a subsequent year of therapy twice weekly. When he entered analysis, he was twenty-seven, married, and had one child. He presented a spectrum of bizarre somatic complaints, together with the idea, not quite of delusional proportions, that his masculinity was deteriorating. He feared that his body was becoming effeminized, that his penis was defective (necessitating masturbation before a mirror), that intercourse would prompt a heart attack, and that he was becoming prematurely senile by virtue of a generalized arteriosclerosis. While acknowledging the irrationality of his symptomatic preoccupations, he continued to mistrust the findings of repeated medical examinations. The onset of his hypochondria could be traced to a period four years earlier when he went abroad, separating temporarily from his fiancée, to embark upon his adult career. Initial data portrayed an "idyllic" childhood. His mother was perceived as omniscient while in reality she proved to be phobic, superstitious, overprotective, and controlling. She also devalued the patient's father, an innocuous presence in his life, and she believed her boy to be better endowed intellectually than he. Only the birth of a baby sister when the patient was five disrupted their bond. The pregnancy and birth were so terrifying for the patient that they precipitated a childhood eating disorder and later an enveloping amnesia for this period in his life. The family's sleeping arangements exposed him to repeated primal scene experiences in the bedroom he shared with his parents until he was eight, then to his sister with whom shared a bedroom until he was twelve, and finally to a nocturnal intimacy of sorts with his rather dull father during adolescence. Exhibitionistic trends were evident in his reminiscences. At the same time his mother repeatedly reprimanded him for masturbating and ridiculed his interest in girls. His first intercourse took place in college with the young woman he eventually married. Leaving her to go aborad precipitated the efflorescence of symptoms.

Revue Française De Psychanalyse. XLII, 1978

The Paradoxes of Schizophrenics. P.-C. Racamier. Pp. 877-969.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

This essay is a synthesis of a number of viewpoints on the schizophrenic process and its relation to narcissism. The author pulls together themes from French writers such as Grunberger, Nacht, Braunschweig, Fain, and Green, as well as his own earlier work. English writers who are considered include Rosenfeld, Winnicott, Little, Macalpine and Hunter, while he considers American views as stated by Searles, Mahler, Kohut, Kernberg, and Jacobson. The result is a learned review of the difficulties threatening the schizophrenic in his encounters with the self and with the object. The theme of a paradox is developed from the concept of the double bind, as one case of many paradoxical binds in which the schizophrenic finds himself. According to Racamier, there is a certain coherence in the means employed by the schizophrenic ego to deal with the reality of things and the object on the one hand, and with the internal reality of self-representations on the other. These methods place the schizophrenic on a path of which the limits are respectively psychotic delusions and narcissistic perversion.

When the Analyst is Chronically Ill or Dying

Eugene Halpert M.D.

Eugene Halpert

Eugene Halpert, M.D.
2 Parkside Drive
Great Neck, N.Y. 11021

Eugene Halpert  

ABSTRACT

This is a study of the effects on the patient, the analyst, and the analytic process of chronic life-threatening illness in the analyst. The vicissitudes of the aggressive drive and its derivatives within the patient are studied in most detail. The analyst's use of denial and isolation, as well as his narcissistic withdrawal in such circumstances, is also illustrated. In addition, some of the practical technical issues which arise are discussed.

Scientific Cosmogony, Mythology, and Immortality

Jacob Arlow M.D.

Jacob Arlow

Jacob A. Arlow, M.D.
120 East 36th St.
New York, N.Y. 10016

Jacob Arlow  

ABSTRACT

Some current scientific theories of cosmogony demonstrate significant similarities to the cosmological theories of mythology and of certain religions. The notion that the universe originated in a specific cataclysmic explosion raises the mental construct of a center of the universe. This concept plays an important role in mythology and is related to the idea of the cyclical renewal of time. Such concepts, both scientific and mythological, serve as reassurance against the fear of extinction. Aspirations to immortality re-emerge in disguised form in the search for life elsewhere in the universe. Some of the cosmological theories resemble metaphorical elaborations of childhood concepts of procreation.

Some Observations on Reality Testing as a Clinical Concept

Sander Abend M.D.

Sander Abend

Sander M. Abend, M.D.
1040 Park Ave.
New York, N.Y. 10028

Sander Abend  

ABSTRACT

This paper asserts that reality testing is a complex ego activity which cannot be characterized globally as either intact or defective. In normals, neurotics, and "borderlines" it is actually a highly variable function. Some problems of nomenclature are addressed. Among many analysts there is an implicit tendency to concretize the means by which reality testing is performed. This may lead to certain conceptual problems and clinical inaccuracies. The relationship of reality testing to unconscious conflicts from all phases of development is emphasized and illustrated. Issues in the technical handling in analysis of manifestations of disturbed reality testing are discussed.

The Perversion of Fetishism in Women

George Zavitzianos M.D.

George Zavitzianos

George Zavitzianos, M.D.
3445 Drummond St.
Montreal, Que. H3G 1X9
Canada

George Zavitzianos  

ABSTRACT

This paper attempts to demonstrate that fetishism as defined by Freud in males also exists among women. Freud described fetishism as a defense against castration anxiety arising from the perception of the female genitals. It is suggested that the main difference between male fetishism and female fetishism is that, because of developmental factors involving the phallic phase, for women the fetish represents the penis of the father, not of the mother. Clinical material is presented to support these hypotheses.

Narrative Truth and Theoretical Truth

Donald Spence

Donald Spence

Donald P. Spence
Rutgers Medical School College of Medicine and Dentistry of New Jersey Department of Psychiatry University Heights
Piscataway, N.J. 08854

Donald Spence  

ABSTRACT

Although Freud was inclined to believe that every effective reconstruction contained a "kernel of truth," it is by no means clear how this kernel can be identified and separated from the set of equally likely fabrications which make up a good part of the patient's life story. If we have no sure way of identifying historical truth, we may be seriously handicapped in our attempt to frame theoretical laws. What may be effective in a particular clinical instance (narrative truth) may not automatically generalize to the larger domain of clinical theory.

Psychoanalytic Theories of Infant Development and its Disturbances: A Critical Evaluation

Sylvia Brody

Sylvia Brody

Sylvia Brody
1148 Fifth Avenue
New York, N.Y. 10028

Sylvia Brody  

ABSTRACT

Various psychoanalytic theories about the emotional and social development of normal infants are current. Each is associated primarily with the individual who has advanced it. Limits are set to the usefulness of the theories by their efforts to comprehend overly broad areas of psychic growth, by their speculative quality, and by their reliance on insufficient data. Progress toward understanding the psychic structure of infants depends upon the coordination of psychoanalytic observations and theory with the studies of infant behaviors being made by developmental and experimental psychologists.

Toward a Psychoanalytic Understanding of Children of Survivors of the Holocaust

Howard Levine M.D.

Howard Levine

Howard B. Levine, M.D.
124 Dean Road
Brookline, Mass. 02146

Howard Levine  

ABSTRACT

The psychoanalytic study of children of survivors of the Holocaust provides the opportunity to contribute to a more effective approach to this population while simultaneously investigating the impact of psychic trauma on personality development. Transgenerational transmission of trauma and the potential developmental consequences of parental affective unavailability and narcissistic overinvestment are examined, with particular emphasis on separation-individuation, superego formation, the management of aggression, and the development of the ego's capacity to maintain an appreciation of the "make-believe" quality of primitive fantasy.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Melanie Klein

By Hanna Segal. New York: Viking Press, 1979. 194 pp.

James Grotstein

James Grotstein

James S. Grotstein
BEVERLY HILLS, CALIF.

James Grotstein  

Melanie Klein has been dead for twenty-one years, and the time has come to re-evaluate her contributions now that the Zeitgeist of current-day psychoanalytic interest seems to be shifting toward the archaic, pregenital lairs of early infancy which she so intrepidly explored from the time of her earliest writings in 1921. This re-evaluation calls for some knowledge about the person, Melanie Klein—about her attitudes, her politics, the life experiences which contributed in some measure to the slant of her contributions—in order to round out our perspective on her work. This is precisely what Hanna Segal has set out to provide.

Melanie Klein's work had a tremendous impact on colleagues in her lifetime and afterwards. Virtually a third of the psychoanalytic world today is either "Kleinian" or has been significantly affected by her work. The rest of the psychoanalytic world has chosen to shun her and her work, at times with an absolutism which even today seems puzzling. Therefore, what influenced her and why her contributions have been so provocative are important questions for psychoanalysts to ponder.

Hanna Segal, one of Melanie Klein's most distinguished analysands (and it should be said that many of her analysands became world famous) has written the sort of book that balances between biographical glimpses and vignettes on the one hand and attention to the development of Klein's technique and theory on the other. Segal has a well-earned reputation as the most lucid and least arcane of Kleinian analysts writing today. Through her pen, the person of Melanie Klein begins to emerge. First of all, Klein was petite, beautiful, feminine, proud—even vain, fearlessly honest, intuitive, and a dedicated product of fin de siècle Vienna. Bion, another of Klein's illustrious analysands, once informed me that she deeply resented having her work referred to as "Kleinian.

[[RunningHead]]

Internal World and External Reality. Object Relations Theory Applied

By Otto F. Kernberg, M.D. New York: Jason Aronson, Inc., 1980. 359 pp.

Victor Calef

Victor Calef

Victor Calef
SAN FRANCISCO

Victor Calef  

To watch and participate in the historical process of the development of ideas is exhilarating as well as hypnotic. To be witness to the unfolding of the thought of one of the most influential exponents and innovators of object relations theory, such as Otto Kernberg, is to become focused on the need and justification for the "widening scope" of psychoanalysis, the nature of psychoanalytic evidence, and the exploration of the similarities and differences between character and symptom.

In this book, Kernberg seeks to illustrate his theoretical understanding of (1) the difficulties encountered by the middle aged; (2) love; (3) small and large groups; and (4) couples. He seems to be responding, at least in part, to the objections of some of his adherents as well as to those of his critics by giving more clinical data, by making his technical recommendations somewhat more explicit, and by elaborating his views about some specific areas of psychological behavior.

In this volume, Kernberg has much more clearly than ever before expressed the nature of his concepts and their derivation. He thus permits a comparison to be drawn between his thoughts and those of others as, for example, between his and Freud's views on affects.

Pathological Defenses in Infancy

Selma Fraiberg

Selma Fraiberg

Selma Fraiberg
Louis Fraiberg 24 Clarendon Ave.
San Francisco, Calif. 94114

Selma Fraiberg  

ABSTRACT

A group of pathological defenses has been observed in infants between three and eighteen months of age who have experienced danger and deprivation to an extreme degree. The early defenses, "avoidance," "freezing," and "fighting," are apparently summoned from a biological repertoire on the model of "flight or fight." Before there is an ego, pain can be transformed into pleasure or obliterated from consciousness while a symptom stands in place of the original conflict.

The Technique of Child Psychoanalysis. Discussions with Anna Freud

By Joseph Sandler, Hansi Kennedy, and Robert L. Tyson. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1980. 277 pp.

Albert Sax

Albert Sax

Albert M. Sax
NEW YORK

Albert Sax  

This excellent book about the practice of child psychoanalysis came to be assembled and written in a unique way. Under the chairmanship of Joseph Sandler and using the case material on the subject of the treatment situation and technique as it is recorded in the Hampstead Psychoanalytic Index, a study group was formed that met weekly for two years. Anna Freud participated in all of the meetings, and all of the discussions were tape recorded and transscribed. This book, arising from the transcriptions, is a distillate of the experience of child psychoanalysis as it is done at the Hampstead Child Therapy Clinic. Miss Freud's comments on a broad range of technical subjects, included verbatim in the book, add immeasurably to the work. They are integrated with the text, most often clarifying the abundant clinical examples which have been used to illustrate the points under examination.

The book provides very interesting reading, in that readers can feel they are participating in the ongoing study and can compare their own ideas with the views at Hampstead. It is designed to be read by those who have an understanding of psychoanalytic concepts as well as a familiarity with age-specific psychosocial and psychosexual development. The book, like the Hampstead Clinic itself, has grown out of the work of Anna Freud. It reflects her perspective that childhood disturbances are deviations from the path of normal development and that psychoanalysis in appropriately chosen cases can restore the child to a normal track.

The book is divided into five parts, each of which is further subdivided into chapters dealing with specific technical issues. The titles of the chapters are actually headings of clinical significance in the Hampstead Psychoanalytic Index. At the beginning of each chapter, there is a note describing how the topics are to be reported for use in the Index for each case included.

A Study on Hysteria: Anna O. Rediviva. W. W. Meissner. Pp. 17-51.

Melvin Stanger

Melvin Stanger

Melvin Stanger  

In a fine paper offering a combination of scholarly research and originality, Meissner nicely summarizes the patient's illness and her treatment by Breuer, delineating the differences between Breuer's and Freud's points of view. He then gives the pertinent biographical data concerning the life and achievements of Bertha Pappenheim. He agrees with Pollock's theses that much of Pappenheim's life and illness really was a form of pathological and delayed mourning. He also concludes that her deep-seated hatred of men had its origins in oedipal disappointments and in an intense sibling rivalry with a younger brother. Meissner takes us beyond the standard psychobiographical approach as he attempts a new integration of the childhood illness and later life of Anna O./Bertha Pappenheim, using the framework supplied by his point of view on the components of the paranoid process elaborated in his earlier works. This involves his ideas concerning core introjects, the projections that derive from them, and the final paranoid construction. this new way of looking at the case of Anna O./Bertha Pappenheim is enlightening and increases our understanding of her illness.

Splitting and Projective Identification

By James S. Grotstein, M.D. New York/London: Aronson, 1981. 236 pp.

George Allison

George Allison

George H. Allison
SEATTLE

George Allison  

In his preface, Grotstein expresses the hope that he can cast light on the operation and interrelationship of the well-known Kleinian concepts which comprise the title of this book. He also states that he intends to "put to rest the alleged differences between projection and projective identification" (p. vii). In addition, he attempts to address classical psychoanalysts as well as Kleinians in the hope of effecting some rapprochement and a fruitful delineation and integration of important conceptual terms and issues. His goals for the most part are not realized, and it is doubtful that either Kleinians or Freudians will find this work clear and comprehensible, much less successful in integrating Kleinian theory (as elaborated by Grotstein) with that of classical authors.

To begin with, Grotstein's understanding and appraisal of the theoretical stance of certain authors is open to question and disagreement.

652

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Thoughts on Psychoanalytic Views of Female Psychology 1927-1977

Jeanne Lampl-De Groot M.D.

Jeanne Lampl-De Groot

Jeanne Lampl-De Groot, M.D.
Haringvlietstraat 39
1078 KA Amsterdam,
Holland

Jeanne Lampl-De Groot  

ABSTRACT

Stimulated by the recent volume on female psychology edited by H. Blum (1977), the author reviews the beginnings of her own interest in the subject more than fifty years ago, particularly her early studies of the preoedipal development of the little girl. Dr. Lampl-de Groot's experience has led her to emphasize the common characteristics in the early development of boys and girls: they both experience curiosity, envy, competition, and jealousy. Only in the phallic-oedipal phase, when rivalries center on the parents, do penis envy and a specific sense of female identity develop in the girl, while boys must resolve their envy of the baby as a prized "product" only the female can produce. Recent literature is criticized, particularly writings by some women authors who attempt to reverse unconscious feelings of inferiority by using recently discovered "facts" of biology for polemical purposes.

responseSet.title: Toward a Methodology for Applying Psychoanalysis to Literature
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Toward a Methodology for Applying Psychoanalysis to Literature

Gail Reed Ph.D.

Gail Reed

Gail S. Reed, Ph.D.
Suite 2E
150 East 93 St.
New York, N. Y. 10028

Gail Reed  

ABSTRACT

This paper proposes a methodology which seeks to use psychoanalysis to fathom the unique quality of the literary text without turning the text into a symptom or its author into a patient. Its hypothesis: the literary text evokes an unconscious fantasy in its readers; critics who respond to the text empathically but without conscious understanding re-enact aspects of its organizing fantasy in the way they write their criticism. To test this hypothesis, the criticism of Jacques le Fataliste et son Maître by Diderot is examined. The phenomenon of parallelism is suggested as a clinical analogy for the re-enactment which takes place.

Freud. Appraisals and Reappraisals. Contributions to Freud Studies, Vol. 1

Edited by Paul E. Stepansky. Hillsdale, NJ: The Analytic Press, 1986, 267 pp.

David Carlson

David Carlson

David A. Carlson
NEW HAVEN, CT

David Carlson  

Paul Stepansky and The Analytic Press have launched a new series of Freud studies, variously informed by archival research, by fresh speculations, and by revisionist reinterpretations, "irrespective of the disciplinary affinities and personal Weltanschauungen of their authors—irrespective, that is, of whose feathers may be ruffled by their work" (p. xvi). The range and feather-ruffling potential of the series is represented by a first volume that opens with a lengthy article by Peter Swales and closes with a short one by John Gedo.

In "Freud: His Teacher and the Birth of Psychoanalysis," Swales sketches the life of Anna von Lieben, with much evidence that she was both the patient referred to as Cäcilie M. in the Studies on Hysteria and the patient Freud described in the autobiographical study as having led him to realize that a deep hypnotic trance was not necessary for catharsis. Swales's argument is convincing, though one is reminded that misidentification of Cäcilie M. began with Fliess ninety years ago.1

Swales offers a less carefully drawn "scenario" of Anna von Lieben's three-year treatment as consisting of daily psychic catharsis, pressure, massage, and probably occasional morphine injections. Still more questionable is Swales's assessment of Anna von Lieben's impact on later psychoanalytic work. Certainly, she was a major source of the young Freud's experience in case management and in the cathartic method, but Swales claims much more for her: that she showed Freud the value of free association, the beginnings of dream interpretation, the role of unconscious sexual symbolism, the tendency of associations to move toward childhood events, conversion, counterwill, conflict, defense, and possibly the clue to the interpretation of wit and superstition. He says she presented Freud with the unconscious "on a silver platter.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Marianne Kris—1900-1980

Samuel Ritvo

Samuel Ritvo

Samuel Ritvo  

Marianne Kris died in her eighty-first year in London on November 23, 1980, at the home of Anna Freud. She had been attending the International Forum of the Hampstead Clinic. The circumstances of her death paralleled the lifelong association of her family with the Freud family. Her father, Dr. Oskar Rie, had been an associate and collaborator of Freud in a child neurology clinic and had been pediatrician to the Freud children.

Dr. Kris was born in Vienna on May 27, 1900. She was graduated in medicine from the University of Vienna in 1925. After two years of psychiatric and psychoanalytic training in Berlin, she returned to Vienna and married Ernst Kris. In the Vienna Institute she was active from the beginning in Anna Freud's seminar on child analysis. When the Nazis took over in Austria in 1938, she and her family moved to London and then came to New York in 1940.

Marianne Kris combined rare personal qualities with superb understanding and skill as a psychoanalyst to make invaluable contributions to the educational and scientific life of the psychoanalytic and child development community wherever she was—the New York Psychoanalytic Institute, the Yale University Child Study Center, the Western New England Institute for Psychoanalysis, and the Columbia University Institute for Psychoanalysis. Her warmth, her interest in students, and her ability to adhere to standards of excellence while appreciating where younger colleagues were in their own development made her an incomparable teacher and supervisor.

In 1950 she joined Dr. Milton Senn and her husband at the Yale University Child Study Center where they were initiating a longitudinal study in child development. This was primarily an action research in which the clinician providing a service was the observer who at the same time influenced the field of observation.

This monograph-size book will appeal to those whose taste runs to dealing abstractly with the abstract. A philosophic reflection on the psychoanalytic interchange, it deals minutely and elegantly with an interpretation of interpretations, an explanation of explanations, the meaning of meaning. At the opposite pole the author seems aware of the desirability of retaining an anchor in the clinical psychoanalytic process. This is not provided, however, with the same intensity or detail as the running theoretical message.

[[RunningHead]]

Alienation in Perversions

By M. Masud R. Khan. New York: International Universities Press, Inc., 1979. 245 pp.

Charles Socarides

Charles Socarides

Charles W. Socarides
NEW YORK

Charles Socarides  

In the last fifteen years Masud Khan has published nearly a dozen psychoanalytic papers on his clinical research and psychoanlaytic treatment of sexually perverse individuals. Until now his highly original and creative efforts have remained scattered throughout the psychoanalytic literature. Some of them were available only in German or French. Others were to be found in relatively hard-to-find journals and books. One of them was published in the London Times Literary Supplement. That we now have all of these frequently cited papers in one volume, readily available for study and easily accessible for reference, is a matter for considerable psychoanalytic rejoicing.

Some of Khan's contributions may seem at first to have been omitted from this valuable collection. When we turn to the "Chronological Bibliography" on page 227, however, we find that many of them have undergone a drastic title change. For example, "Foreskin Fetishism and Its Relation to Ego Pathology in a Male Homosexual," originally published in the International Journal of Psychoanalysis, Vol. 46 (1965), now appears as "Fetish as Negation of the Self: Clinical Notes on Foreskin Fetishism in a Male Homosexual, Part One." In another instance, the title of a paper that at first was published in French bears no resemblance to the original French title; "Ne pas se souvenir de sois même" is translated into "From Masochism to Psychic Pain." This slight inconvenience for the reader could well have been avoided if both titles had been given in the table of contents.

Khan notes that whereas perversion protects the patient, the very success of the mechanism not only alienates him from others but keeps him "alienated from his self" (p. 176). Removing the perverse symptom leaves the patient subject to a deep "sense of emptiness." This may be considered a "hazard of the psychoanalytic cure" (Khan), although by relieving the deeper anxieties out of which perversion evolves, we may help the patient find a life which is meaningful, "sentient and true," with purpose as well as direction.

The Mind of Watergate. An Exploration of the Compromise of Integrity

By Leo Rangell, M.D. New York: W.W. Norton & Co., Inc., 1980. 318 pp.

George Pollock

George Pollock

George H. Pollock
CHICAGO

George Pollock  

This is a very difficult book to review. It touches on many issues of importance to thinking individuals, and yet it has a unique methodological approach that raises questions. As he suggests in the title, Rangell seeks to explore the phenomenon of compromise of integrity by studying the Watergate incident. Yet he notes that he had "no private information about any of the individuals involved in the Watergate phenomenon." He obtained "all the data in this book … from public sources" (p. 305). I understand what he means, but it is inevitable that his own responses, as well as those of his colleagues, patients, and friends, should make a contribution to his "data." He does study "the manner in which what was available was distorted, or not received at all." Questions have to be raised about the reliability of information that is mainly derived from the media—especially from newspapers and magazines.

By Herbert S. Strean. New York: The Free Press, 1979. 240 pp.

Irving Kaufman

Irving Kaufman

Irving Kaufman
NEWTON, MASS.

Irving Kaufman  

Strean has written a very readable book relating psychoanalytic concepts to social work. The first chapter consists of an overview. It contains an extremely interesting history of the impact of psychoanalysis on social work practice. There has been a rise and fall in the role played by psychoanalytic concepts in social work. In the 1920's and 1930's psychoanalytic concepts dominated social work theory and humanized its practice. Gradually the psychoanalytic conceptualization of human behavior has been replaced by other frames of reference. Focus on family interaction, role theory, issues of poverty, social discrimination, etc., have moved closer to the foreground.

DISCUSSION: Dr. Aaron H. Esman felt that the authors' data were impressive and fascinating, but he found fault with a too ready leap from observed behavior to presumed mental activity, which risks the errors of adultomorphism, reductionism, and misattribution. Certainly the data offered are susceptible to alternative interpretations. The authors seem to pay scant attention to ego developmental and object relations perspectives, tending to assign primacy to the area of sexual development. Dr. Esman expressed the hope that the authors will use their data to explicate the interrelationships of psychosexual development and object relations development. Dr. John McDevitt saw a need to integrate Mahler's studies on separation-individuation with the authors' wealth of data on psychosexual development. He noted that much of the data must have been obtained by questioning the parents. What effect might this have had on the parents and what influence might it have had on their observations and answers? He would expect a wider range of individual differences in development. He felt also that the boys' reaction to observations of genital differences is more complicated than just denial. He found very interesting the positive relationship between the us of denial and the capacity for symbolic elaboration. Other variables may be important as well—for example, the nature and degree of elaboration of symbolic play. The boys' play may be equally symbolic but less rich and accessible, thereby giving the appearance of less fantasy elaboration.

[[RunningHead]]

The Power of Form. A Psychoanalytic Approach to Aesthetic Form. (Psychological Issues, Monograph 49.)

By Gilbert J. Rose. New York: International Universities Press, Inc., 1980. 233 pp.

Leon Balter

Leon Balter

Leon Balter
NEW YORK

Leon Balter  

The relation of psychoanalysis to art has always been uneasy for many different reasons. Probably the most important is that artistic products and the process of their creation are not investigated to any great degree in the psychoanalytic situation—or, if they are, there is no systematic reporting of them. The analysis of artists produces other kinds of data, such as their conflicts, their childhoods, their interpersonal and object relationships. Whatever the reasons, the work of Ernst Kris and Phyllis Greenacre is the worthy standard by which to judge what psychoanalysts do, or can do, in that realm.

Gilbert Rose's book, The Power of Form, is not in the path blazed by Kris and Greenacre. He subtitles his book, "A Psychoanalytic Approach to Aesthetic Form." It is psychoanalytic, but it is withdrawn from the person of the artist and the person of the appreciator. The central subject of Rose's treatise is the artistic product itself and the "space" between it and the above two people. Psychoanalysts, who, after all, deal with people, may be put off by Rose's thesis. Nevertheless, it deserves serious consideration.

Rose's theory of aesthetic creativity and aesthetic experience is concerned solely with form, quite divorced from content. Motives (drive discharge and defense in the context of conflict) are excluded from Rose's discussion because motives are a part of content. He is pointedly explicit about this and acknowledges that his orientation is a departure from the standard psychoanalytic approach that principally addresses motives. Because Rose avoids motive-content, his formulations must utilize corresponding psychological terms which describe more formal, relatively nonconflictual aspects of mental functioning. [[RunningHead]]

Returning to Freud: Clinical Psychoanalysis in the School of Lacan

Edited and translated by Stuart Schneiderman. New Haven: Yale University Press, 1980. 260 pp.

John Muller

John Muller

John P. Muller
STOCKBRIDGE, MASS.

John Muller  

This book attempts to fill an obvious gap in the Lacanian psychoanalytic literature available in English. The question often is asked, "What do Lacanian analysts do when they practice clinical psychoanalysis?" There is a growing body of material in English that explores Lacanian theoretical formulations that have been so influential in Paris and elsewhere in Europe for the past twenty-five

461

years, but until now published clinical material in English has been almost nonexistent.

The book consists of two brief introductory essays by the editor/translator, the transcript of an interview conducted by Lacan with a psychotic patient, and a series of fifteen papers by members of Lacan's former institute. These papers were published in French during the years 1956 to 1979 in a variety of journals and books associated with the work of the institute.

The introductory essays by the editor provide a useful overview of the Lacanian framework. The text of the Lacan interview (which runs for twenty-two pages) is here published for the first time (it has not been published in French) and provides a rare glimpse of Lacan's clinical style. The most impressive (and perhaps reassuring) feature lies in its respectable ordinariness. Except for a few passages that highlight homophonies, the interview is a sober exchange between a hospitalized patient and a visiting doctor, conducted for teaching purposes. What does it teach? Lacan himself later refers to the patient as an example of "a 'Lacanian' psychosis" (p. 41), and the patient (who had read some of Lacan's work) provides abundant examples of Lacanian themes. He refers to himself as being "a little disjointed in regard to language" (p. 19), his auditory hallucinations are "imposed speech … which has no meaning in the ordinary sense" (p. 20), he self-aggrandizes by homophonically reconstructing his name, and he distinguishes "the imaginary" from "the real" and counterposes to both the realm of speech: "All speech has the force of law; all speech is signifying" (p. 23). The patient goes on to describe his position as being at the center of a solitary circle and as living without boundaries. In Schreber-like fashion, he reports having thought that his phallus was shrinking, that he was going to become a woman, and that he has been the object of thought transmission. He contracts words, coins neologisms, and makes antiphonal responses to imposed sentences—all of this fitting nicely with Lacan's own analysis of the Schreber text in his Écrits. The post-interview remarks, unfortunately, strike the sort of pessimistic tone that could lend weight to the arguments proposed in some Lacanian quarters that analytic treatment of psychosis is pointless (although Jacques-Alain Miller rightly cautions against "the spontaneous activism of those who devote themselves to psychotics" [p. 44]).

The Annual of Psychoanalysis. VII, 1978

Death Anxiety and Adaptation to Mortality in Psychoanalytic Theory. Irwin Hoffman. Pp. 233-267.

Melvin Stanger

Melvin Stanger

Melvin Stanger  

This is a thoughtful article in an area that has been rather neglected by psychoanalysts. The author questions Freud's position on awareness of death and death anxiety. How can the unconscious be convinced of its own immortality when it is oblivious to time? How can we not believe in our own death

477

when we in fact avoid facing it because of the narcissistic injury involved? Hoffman suggests that there is instead a conscious belief in immortality which is defensive against an unconscious fear of death. Hoffman agrees with Kohut that the fear of death represents the destruction of the nuclear self, but he also reproves him for not integrating this anxiety within Freud's genetic hierarchy of anxiety experiences. The author postulates a more advanced ego level that is achievable, in which tolerance of ambivalent feelings about death can exist. Here existential "dread" and anticipatory mourning, as well as self-affirmation, occur. Hoffman reached his views through work with parents who have had to deal with a fatal illness (leukemia) in their child. The author was impressed by the ability of parents to live with simultaneous contradictions and ambiguity. These parents could affirm faith in the self and yet experience profound skepticism, doubt, and anger. The work of mourning became increasingly focused on the quality of the child's life and of the time spent with her or him, in lieu of the amount of time lost, and thus a change in the quality of investment in both the lost object and in potential new objects appeared to be an important outcome of this process. Hoffman points out that the course of adaptation to mortality should be further investigated clinically through analytic work with older patients, since the heightened sense of "time running out" is likely to resonate with previous kinds of threats to the integrity of the self and is likely to stir up early developmental conflicts. The author concludes by stating his belief that this entire subject can be most usefully studied with a perspective that integrates the existential point of view with the classical psychoanalytic hierarchy of danger situations.

Boundary and Space. An Introduction to the Work of D. W. Winnicott

By Madeleine Davis and David Wallbridge. New York: Brunner/Mazel, 1981. 196 pp.

Simon Grolnick

Simon Grolnick

Simon A. Grolnick
GREAT NECK, N.Y.

Simon Grolnick  

Once Donald Winnicott remarked to a group of his students: "What you get out of me, you will have to pick out of chaos." Winnicott's chaos, however, like Freud's id, is not truly an amorphous vacuum; nor is it, as Ovid termed chaos in Metamorphoses, an "undigestible lump." When opposed to the Cosmos, or ordered universe, Chaos can refer to that region between heaven and earth, according to the Encyclopaedia Britannica. This is a definition that is not far from Winnicott's paradoxical, symbolic, playful space between reality and fantasy, an area that he worked within as well as conceptualized. I think that Winnicott's creative style allowed him to provide only a part of the organization of his ideas—the rest he asked for from his readers.

Any author who attempts to structure Winnicott's ideas accepts a significant challenge. The authors of Boundary and Space apologize for the book's being "not altogether tidy," stating that "one section will invade another, and repetitions occur." They explain: "With Winnicott it is particularly difficult to separate idea from idea, and impossible, as we have mentioned, to separate the ideas from the man" (p. xi). Those of us who have entered into a dialogue with the textual Winnicott cannot help but agree.

Boundary and Space attempts to present a rather text-near explication of Winnicott and, by doing so, to stimulate the reader to read Winnicott himself. Here the authors can be commended: they have accomplished their goal. Fortunately, they have been assisted greatly by Clare Winnicott, who provided them with access to much fascinating unpublished material, enriching quotes from which are sprinkled throughout the book.

Unfortunately, in their attempt to introduce and present Winnicott to the reader, the authors use Winnicott's own titles and metaphorical language for their organization.

Adult Development. A New Dimension in Psychodynamic Theory and Practice

By Calvin A. Colarusso, M.D. and Robert A. Nemiroff, M.D. New York/London: Plenum Press, 1981. 290 pp.

Rebecca Solomon

Rebecca Solomon

Rebecca Z. Solomon
HARTFORD, CONN.

Rebecca Solomon  

The authors' purpose in writing this book was to delineate the normal development of adulthood and to indicate the relationship between faulty development and psychopathology. They undertook this task because they found developmental concepts very useful in their work as clinicians and educators.

In the book they trace interest in human development back to antiquity. The writings, ceremonials, and rituals of many cultures and civilizations attest to such interest in ancient times, but development was not systematically studied until recently. Freud stressed the importance of development in childhood. Jung viewed development as a process which continues throughout life. In the past two decades the developmental tasks of adulthood have been studied by Erikson, Gould, Levinson, and Vaillant, among others.

On the basis of their review of historical and transcultural accounts of attitudes toward adulthood, their examination of recent studies on the subject by others, and their own observations, the authors offer several hypotheses about developmental issues in adulthood. They postulate that development is a dynamic process which is ongoing throughout life, i.e., that the same process extends throughout childhood and adulthood. Adult development, they indicate, is focused on the evolution and alteration of existing psychic structures. Physical, physiological, and psychological events that occur during adulthood influence the course of adult development. The authors warn against reductionistic interpretations of adult behavior that depict it as only a manifestation of infantile experience or as only a response to current happenings. They stress a dynamic interaction between current experience and existing psychic structures which are the result of preceding development.

On Discovering Mother has a First Name

Samuel Abrams M.D.

Samuel Abrams

Samuel Abrams, M.D.
25 East 83rd St.
New York, N.Y. 10028

Samuel Abrams  

A young woman who had always been viewed as precociously mature in her relationships responded to the information that I would be absent for a week by asking a series of personal questions. She wanted to know if I was married, whether I had children, where I lived, and what I would be doing during that week and with whom. When I suggested that her thoughts about the questions might be more useful than the answers, she felt somewhat rebuffed—although she disavowed any discomfort. She went on to speak about her closeness to her mother. The two of them had a marvelous thing, she said; they were more like confidantes than mother and daughter. Each could discuss topics with the other that she imagined most relatives customarily avoided. Their long talks were reminiscent of college roommates. The two of them were truly "friends."

A childhood memory surfaced suddenly; it had been unavailable until that moment. At first it seemed to her only a trivial recollection. When she was three, her mother had been depressed following the birth of a new child. The depression had caused her to become remote and relatively unavailable for a period of time. The patient had no memory of all of this, although she had heard about it from her parents on quite a few occasions. The new memory that was hers at the moment was the recollection that during that period she had discovered that her mother had a first name—Gloria. Mother was not only "mommy"; she was also "Gloria." She recalled how excited she was about the discovery; and then she wondered about the surfacing of the memory in the session.

The Voice of Conscience and the Sounds of the Analytic Hour

Martin Silverman M.D.

Martin Silverman

Martin Silverman  

ABSTRACT

Two patients reacted to sudden, unexpected, adventitious sounds during an analytic session as though they had been warned that they would be punished for their misdeeds. One promptly confessed to wrongdoings which she had been denying or keeping secret. It was as though a "voice of conscience" had spoken to them to remind them of their obligations, demand compliance with the rules, and threaten them with dire punishments should they fail to obey. The sounds seemed to be experienced as a re-externalized admonishing parental voice that had been incompletely internalized in the course of superego development. Conflicts involving guilt over objectionable fantasies and acts, in part connected with primal scene experiences, appeared to be involved.
